rule: two independent readers of the full texts agree (both blind readers, or one reader and a third who checked the source); quotes checked verbatim in code

alex-karp.q: Indeed, if we fail to act, to formulate an affirmative view of what technology can accomplish, the undirected logic of the market will decide for us
alex-karp.why: He says society can and should choose what technology accomplishes rather than leave it to an undirected process.

alondra-nelson.q: It is not inevitable that AI will lead to great public benefits. The outcomes many of us hope for, or anticipate, are not inherent features of the technology itself. They are not coded into algorithms, or embedded in neural networks.
alondra-nelson.work: Three Fallacies: Alondra Nelson's Remarks at Élysée Palace on the Occasion of the AI Action Summit
alondra-nelson.why: Presented as a fallacy to be corrected, she denies that AI's outcomes are fixed by the technology and goes on to say they must be stewarded through leadership and democratic institutions.

arvind-narayanan.q: It rejects technological determinism, especially the notion of AI itself as an agent in determining its future.
arvind-narayanan.why: The authors reject technological determinism and stress that institutions shape AI's trajectory.

audrey-tang.q: So the question here, in this spinning wheel, is not whether we should accelerate AI or stop AI. It is who should steer that spinning wheel.
audrey-tang.work: 2025-11-10 Berlin Freedom Conference: The Role of AI
audrey-tang.why: She frames AI's social effects as a matter of collective steering, contrasting a default trajectory with one people choose together.

bernie-sanders.q: Congress must act to ensure AI benefits all of us—not just a handful of billionaires racing forward for power and profit.
bernie-sanders.work: Artificial intelligence is coming for the working class. We must fight back
bernie-sanders.why: He treats who benefits from AI as a matter for legislative choice, listing policies that would change its effects on workers.

brian-merchant.q: We’re left at a crossroads where we must consider nothing less than what kind of jobs we want people to be able to do, what kind of work and which institutions we think are important as a society, and what we’re willing to do to protect them
brian-merchant.work: The AI jobs crisis is here, now
brian-merchant.why: He frames AI's effect on work as the product of management decisions and a societal choice about what work to protect, not an inevitable process.

daron-acemoglu.q: So the first thing I do, therefore, is to argue against technological determinism.
daron-acemoglu.work: Mindscape 283: Daron Acemoglu on Technology, Inequality, and Power
daron-acemoglu.why: Explaining the thesis of Power and Progress, he says there is no predetermined path of technological progress and its direction depends on how we use our collective knowledge.

dean-ball.q: The future does not unfold by show of hands, not even in a democracy. The decaying structures of high industrialism do not stand a chance in this conflict, which has been ongoing for decades and which they have been losing for the duration of that period.
dean-ball.why: He says outright that the course of the AI transformation is not set by collective decision, and treats its direction as beyond the reach of existing institutions.

demis-hassabis.q: And the future in my view is still to be written, but these next few years are going to be very critical as to which way that will go and how we collectively want that to look like.
demis-hassabis.work: Demis Hassabis Thinks We're in the 'Foothills of the Singularity'
demis-hassabis.why: He frames the outcome of the AGI transition as open and set by collective choices in the coming years.

divya-siddarth.q: Technology expands what we are capable of. Democracy is how we decide what to do with that capability.
divya-siddarth.work: How AI and Democracy Can Fix Each Other (transcript)
divya-siddarth.why: She holds that what technology does to society is decided collectively through democracy.

e-glen-weyl.q: But neither is it predetermined. There are clusters of plausible visions of the future and technologies that empower these; through our collective technological investments, we help choose among these possibilities.
e-glen-weyl.why: In the authors' own voice, the range of technological futures is not predetermined and is chosen through collective investment.

emily-m-bender.q: With all of the resources being poured into LLMs (and similarly into very large models trained on image datasets), it’s worth remembering that nothing is predestined about this.
emily-m-bender.work: On NYT Magazine on AI: Resist the Urge to be Impressed
emily-m-bender.why: She says the current technological path is not inevitable and other futures can be chosen.

holly-elmore.q: The right and the power to curb dangerous AI development is already ours!
holly-elmore.work: YOU have the power: my Stop the AI Race speech
holly-elmore.why: She tells protestors that citizens collectively have the power to decide AI's course, not the companies or an inevitable race.

jack-clark.q: I work on AI because whether it does that is about choices we make - choices people here in this room will make - about how we direct it and how we govern it.
jack-clark.work: Import AI 477: In which I tell the IMF the Singularity has begun
jack-clark.why: The author says whether AI's benefits are realised depends on collective choices about how to direct and govern it.

jd-vance.q: But all of this, the role that technology plays in a labor market, and whether we greet innovative breakthroughs with excitement or with trepidation depends on the purpose of our economic system in the first place.
jd-vance.work: Remarks by the Vice President at the American Dynamism Summit
jd-vance.why: He says how technology affects labor depends on how we set up the economy, which is a collective choice.

josh-hawley.q: But this is only one possible future; not the future. We can achieve something different.
josh-hawley.why: After describing AI's current course, he says that course is not fixed and can be changed by collective action.

karen-hao.q: These are all different ways that people are contesting how AI has been developed, how it's being deployed, and can actually actively use these different levers to shape the way AI continues to develop and get deployed in the future.
karen-hao.why: She argues collective action can shape how AI develops and is deployed.

max-tegmark.q: the rest of my talk is going to be about the good news, that it's not inevitable, and we can absolutely do better, alright?
max-tegmark.work: How to Keep AI Under Control
max-tegmark.why: Against the 'it's inevitable' framing, he says the course of AI is not fixed and can be changed.

meredith-whittaker.q: critical and actually regain a bit more of our own agency in relationship to mythologies that  kind of naturalize these systems as just a sort of linear arc of technological and human progress.
meredith-whittaker.work: Meredith Whittaker on Who Controls Your Data in the Age of AI
meredith-whittaker.why: She argues that we can choose which technologies to use and rejects the idea that AI follows a natural, linear course of progress.

mustafa-suleyman.q: This is a story that's still unfolding. Nothing should be accepted as a given. We all must choose what we create.
mustafa-suleyman.why: He says what AI becomes is not a given and depends on collective choice about what to build or allow.

nick-land.q: The profound institutional crisis that makes the topic ‘hot’ has at its core an implosion of social decision-making capability. Doing anything, at this point, would take too long. So instead, events increasingly just happen.
nick-land.why: He argues that collective decision-making is collapsing and that accelerating change now simply happens rather than being chosen.

paul-kingsnorth.q: This thing - this technological nervous system, this technium, this gollem, this Machine - has a life of its own.
paul-kingsnorth.why: He argues the digital revolution follows its own momentum rather than human collective decision, echoing his claim elsewhere that technology 'has a direction of travel'.

pope-leo-xiv.q: In practice, however, technology is never neutral, because it takes on the characteristics of those who devise, finance, regulate and use it.
pope-leo-xiv.work: Magnifica Humanitas: Encyclical on safeguarding the human person in the time of Artificial Intelligence
pope-leo-xiv.why: He holds that technology's effects are shaped by human choices about design, finance, regulation and use, framing the issue as a choice between Babel and Jerusalem.

timnit-gebru.q: Only when we change the incentive structure will we see technology that prioritizes the wellbeing of citizens
timnit-gebru.work: For truly ethical AI, its research must be independent from big tech
timnit-gebru.why: She treats the direction of technology as set by changeable incentives and public funding choices, not a fixed course.

vitalik-buterin.q: We need active human intention to choose the directions that we want, as the formula of "maximize profit" will not arrive at them automatically.
vitalik-buterin.why: He argues the direction of technology must be chosen deliberately rather than left to an automatic process.

william-macaskill.q: The nature of the constraints from competition and human goals can be affected by what has happened earlier in AI development and deployment. Multiple equilibria are possible.
william-macaskill.why: Answering the claim that competitive pressure fixes AI's shape, he argues outcomes are path-dependent and can be steered by choices and public opinion.

alex-karp.q: The war in eastern Europe stems from a collective suspension of disbelief by those whose overconfidence in recent decades in the raw power of their ideals enabled the balance of power in Europe to shift.
alex-karp.work: In Defense of Europe (A Letter from the Chief Executive Officer)
alex-karp.why: He blames the war on overconfidence in the power of ideals, arguing hard power is needed.

dario-amodei.q: I think the Culture’s values are a winning strategy because they’re the sum of a million small decisions that have clear moral force and that tend to pull everyone together onto the same side.
dario-amodei.why: He says liberal, humane values tend to win out on their own moral force, though elsewhere he stresses that democracy's triumph still requires effort.

demis-hassabis.q: I think we can't take for granted anymore democratic values are going to win out—I don’t think that's clear at all.
demis-hassabis.work: Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis on AGI and AI in the Military
demis-hassabis.why: He explicitly denies that democratic values can be relied on to prevail, citing serious threats in a more dangerous world.

leopold-aschenbrenner.q: The free world must prevail over the authoritarian powers in this race. We owe our peace and freedom to American economic and military preeminence.
leopold-aschenbrenner.work: IIId. The Free World Must Prevail
leopold-aschenbrenner.why: He attributes the survival of freedom to economic and military power rather than to the force of liberal ideals themselves.

samuel-hammond.q: This makes liberal democracy as we know it the byproduct of a contingent technological equilibrium; one that AI is almost certainly going to change.
samuel-hammond.why: He argues liberal democracy depends on contingent institutional and technological conditions rather than prevailing by the force of its ideals.

alex-karp.q: The engineering elite of Silicon Valley may know more than most about building software. But they do not know more about how society should be organized or what justice requires.
alex-karp.work: Letter from the Chief Executive Officer (Palantir S-1)
alex-karp.why: Asking where authority over technology should reside, he denies it to unelected tech elites and ties his work to the survival of democratic government.

alondra-nelson.q: the best-case scenario is I think a public that's awakened to these issues and that really refuses a narrative that says that if you don't have a PhD in AI from MIT or in computer science that you can't have a say about how these technologies are going to be built and used.
alondra-nelson.work: A Conversation with Dr. Alondra Nelson on AI and Democracy
alondra-nelson.why: Her best case is a public that rejects rule by technical experts and claims its own say over the technology, which matches putting authority with popular self-government.

audrey-tang.q: The 6-Pack’s reliance on bridging, deliberation, and alignment assemblies is expressive-collaborative morality in practice: moral norms emerge from democratic encounter, not from expert decree
audrey-tang.why: She grounds the norms that govern AI in citizen deliberation rather than expert decree, and elsewhere says 'We cannot delegate democracy.'

bernie-sanders.q: The future of humanity cannot be left in the hands of a few Big Tech oligarchs who are obsessed with money and power. The American people and people throughout the world must determine that future.
bernie-sanders.work: Don't Let Big Tech Dictate Humanity's Future
bernie-sanders.why: He says the people, not unelected tech executives, must decide AI's future.

brian-merchant.q: A big question of the AI age, to me, is whether it’s possible to subject the ultra-powerful interests currently guiding AI deployment
brian-merchant.work: Understanding the Luddites in the age of AI
brian-merchant.why: He wants AI's powerful owners subjected to a truly democratic process, and elsewhere condemns the 'profound antidemocratic tendency' of the AI project.

curtis-yarvin.q: One conclusion of formalism is that democracy is—as most writers before the 19th century agreed—an ineffective and destructive system of government.
curtis-yarvin.why: In his own manifesto he calls democracy ineffective and destructive and favors rule by owners of the state.

daniel-kokotajlo.q: The tail-risk scenarios in which a tiny group leverages AGI to gain unprecedented power over everyone else in society and the world become less likely, because the rest of society will be more in the know about what’s happening.
daniel-kokotajlo.work: Training AGI in Secret would be Unsafe and Unethical
daniel-kokotajlo.why: He warns against corporate leaders and executive-branch officials holding unaccountable power, and hopes power is devolved 'in a democratic fashion'.

daron-acemoglu.q: excessive reliance on technocracy, without citizen input, may also start encroaching into political decisions
daron-acemoglu.why: In a section on technocracy versus democracy, he warns that delegating political decisions to algorithms or technocrats without citizen input would undermine democracy.

divya-siddarth.q: We are told that transformative technologies like AI are too complicated, or too risky or too important to be governed democratically. But this is precisely why they must be.
divya-siddarth.work: How AI and Democracy Can Fix Each Other (transcript)
divya-siddarth.why: She argues AI must be governed democratically rather than left to experts, while also wanting to evolve democratic institutions.

e-glen-weyl.q: Technocracy divorced from the need for public communication and accountability is thus a dangerous ideology that distracts technical experts from the valuable role they can play by tempting them to assume undue, independent power and influence.
e-glen-weyl.work: Why I Am Not A Technocrat
e-glen-weyl.why: The essay's conclusion is that expert rule without democratic accountability is dangerous and that experts belong inside a broader democratic conversation.

holly-elmore.q: The governance of superintelligence has to represent the stakeholders of Earth— all people. AI companies cannot grade their own homework. They cannot be allowed to hold so much power that they eclipse democracy.
holly-elmore.work: YOU have the power: my Stop the AI Race speech
holly-elmore.why: She insists that democratic, representative authority, not unelected AI companies, must govern AI.

jd-vance.q: It is the business of democracy to adjudicate these big questions at the ballot box.
jd-vance.work: Remarks at the Munich Security Conference
jd-vance.why: He insists big political questions belong to voters, criticising leaders who ignore or override them.

josh-hawley.q: A country governed by experts is not self-governing. A country governed by oligarchs is not a republic.
josh-hawley.work: The American Covenant’s Answer to AI
josh-hawley.why: He rejects rule by experts or tech leaders and argues for the people governing themselves.

karen-hao.q: Empires are antithetical to democracy, and allowing these companies to just do whatever they want, have access to embedded resources, over time will lead to the erosion of our foundation of democracy.
karen-hao.why: She defends democracy against rule by unaccountable corporate power.

leopold-aschenbrenner.q: The radical proposal is not The Project; the radical proposal is taking a bet on private AI CEOs wielding military power and becoming benevolent dictators.
leopold-aschenbrenner.why: In arguing that democratic governments, not unelected CEOs, should control superintelligence, he rejects rule by unaccountable executives.

meredith-whittaker.q: meaning that the people who are getting elected to federal office in particular, have to appeal to those who have billions of dollars if they want the resources they need to compete. That's an anti-democratic step.
meredith-whittaker.work: Tech, AI, digital infrastructure and surveillance with Meredith Whittaker
meredith-whittaker.why: She condemns the shift of political power from voters to billionaires and multinational corporations as anti-democratic, and calls for more democratic governance of technology.

nick-land.q: Democracy, which both in theory and evident historical fact accentuates time-preference to the point of convulsive feeding-frenzy, is thus as close to a precise negation of civilization as anything could be
nick-land.why: In his own unattributed argument (not a quotation of Moldbug or Hoppe), Land calls democracy close to the negation of civilization.

sam-altman.q: It is important that the democratic process remains more powerful than companies.
sam-altman.work: Untitled post, shown on the blog as "-"
sam-altman.why: He says the democratic process must stay more powerful than AI companies and that a few labs should not decide the future.

yoshua-bengio.q: It is thus imperative that we find ways to navigate solutions that avoid such paths that would destroy democracy
yoshua-bengio.why: Rejecting a surveillance dictatorship as a response to AI risk, he insists solutions must preserve democracy.

alondra-nelson.q: Through deliberate and thoughtful governance, U.S. and EU policymakers can guide AI development toward systems that amplify, rather than erode, rights and dignity
alondra-nelson.work: Regulating AI in the Evolving Transatlantic Landscape
alondra-nelson.why: She endorses government policymakers steering the direction of AI development, the opposite of keeping it free of state direction.

daniel-kokotajlo.q: Amodei, Altman, and Musk have all agreed on the need to “pace the frontier.” But they haven’t meaningfully paced the frontier yet. I think that the US government should intervene.
daniel-kokotajlo.why: In his Senate testimony he asks the government to step in and steer how frontier AI development proceeds.

daron-acemoglu.q: We see nine ways that public policy could channel advances in AI toward being pro-worker if desired.
daron-acemoglu.why: Arguing that the market undersupplies pro-worker AI, the paper proposes public policy to steer the direction of AI development, though elsewhere he cautions against government acting as the innovator itself.

david-sacks.q: In my view, the most likely dystopian outcome with AI is a marriage of corporate and state power similar to what we saw exposed in the Twitter Files, where “Trust & Safety” gets weaponized into government censorship and control.
david-sacks.work: Long X post: the 'Goldilocks' state of AI and why the doomer narratives were wrong
david-sacks.why: He names government control of AI, fused with corporate power, as the most likely dystopia to avoid.

dean-ball.q: Of course government cannot assume control over the development of this technology or over the firms that develop it.
dean-ball.work: 2023 (Or, Why I am Not a Doomer)
dean-ball.why: He states that government must not control AI development or the firms that do it, and elsewhere calls state monopolization of advanced AI the ultimate dystopia.

elon-musk.q: And if a new model is very dangerous and the company producing that model is not taking steps to address the danger, then they should alert the government to take action to limit the release of that model.
elon-musk.work: Full Transcript: Zanny Minton Beddoes Interviews Elon Musk (The Economist)
elon-musk.why: He wants governments to step in and limit the release of dangerous frontier models, which is state control over AI development.

guillaume-verdon.q: And so I just want separation of AI and state
guillaume-verdon.work: Guillaume Verdon: Beff Jezos, E/acc Movement, Physics, Computation & AGI (Lex Fridman Podcast #407)
guillaume-verdon.why: He states the position directly, warning against a government-backed AI cartel.

holly-elmore.q: This adds friction to the already uphill process of establishing who’s boss (our democracy) and getting regulation on the AI industry.
holly-elmore.why: She wants democratic government to be 'boss' over the AI industry through regulation, rejecting the idea that AI development should stay free of state control.

leopold-aschenbrenner.q: There are no good options here—but I don’t see another way. When a technology becomes this important for national security, we will need the USG.
leopold-aschenbrenner.why: He argues that AGI development must come under US government direction through a national project.

pope-leo-xiv.q: a just social order guarantees everyone equal access to opportunities, protects the youngest and weakest members of society, combats hate and misinformation and subjects the use of data and technology to public oversight
pope-leo-xiv.work: Magnifica Humanitas: Encyclical on safeguarding the human person in the time of Artificial Intelligence
pope-leo-xiv.why: He wants technology placed under public oversight, and laments that private actors have replaced the state in guiding innovation.

sam-altman.q: The two obvious ways to do this are individual empowerment and making sure democratic system stays in control.
sam-altman.work: Untitled post, shown on the blog as "-"
sam-altman.why: He wants the democratic system to stay in control of AGI, and elsewhere calls for government regulation of its development.

yoshua-bengio.q: both groups want government intervention to protect the public, which means some form of regulation and public oversight of AI.
yoshua-bengio.work: Reasoning through arguments against taking AI safety seriously
yoshua-bengio.why: The author, who counts himself among those worried about AI risk, calls for government regulation and public oversight of AI development.

alondra-nelson.q: looming risks such as exacerbating bias, catalyzing labor disruption, increasing surveillance, and widening inequality—heightens the urgency for meaningful and enforceable guardrails.
alondra-nelson.work: Regulating AI in the Evolving Transatlantic Landscape
alondra-nelson.why: She calls for enforceable, government-set guardrails on AI, which includes binding rules on the companies that develop it.

bernie-sanders.q: We must place an immediate pause on advanced-AI development and ban artificial superintelligence
bernie-sanders.work: Don't Let Big Tech Dictate Humanity's Future
bernie-sanders.why: He calls for a legislated pause and ban, overseen by a new federal body, which are binding rules on frontier developers.

brian-merchant.q: California’s the best hope for strong AI regulation, yet the governor’s political aspirations will keep him cozy with Silicon Valley.
brian-merchant.work: The Luddite Renaissance is in full swing
brian-merchant.why: He treats strong AI regulation as something to hope for, and elsewhere criticises OpenAI for lobbying against state AI laws and product liability.

daniel-kokotajlo.q: Get companies to make voluntary commitments, and government to make regulation / executive orders, that include public reporting requirements, aimed at making it impossible to do it in secret without violating these commitments.
daniel-kokotajlo.work: Training AGI in Secret would be Unsafe and Unethical
daniel-kokotajlo.why: His policy recommendation includes government regulation that imposes reporting requirements on AGI developers.

dario-amodei.q: Addressing the risks of AI will require a mix of voluntary actions taken by companies (and private third-party actors) and actions taken by governments that bind everyone.
dario-amodei.why: He says government actions binding everyone will be required, though he wants them judicious and limited for now.

daron-acemoglu.q: In theory, when automation is excessive and AI research is not being directed to creating new tasks, welfare-promoting regulation should discourage automation at the margin and encourage the creation of new labor-intensive tasks.
daron-acemoglu.why: In the section on technology choice and regulation, he argues that unregulated AI innovation will not self-correct and that regulation should steer the direction of AI development.

dean-ball.q: The medium-term solution to the broader problem—the lack of a coherent frontier AI governance framework—is a technocratic law, passed by Congress and not by Executive fiat, that puts real guardrails on both industry and government.
dean-ball.work: Leviathan Waking (On Anthropic/USG, and a new era in AI governance)
dean-ball.why: He calls for a law passed by Congress that puts real guardrails on frontier AI companies; elsewhere he backs SB 53 and federalizing the state frontier-safety laws.

demis-hassabis.q: And I think some form of really almost a smart regulation is required that is dynamic and can adapt with the times very quickly, and probably informed by the leading labs because they’re seeing what’s actually at the coalface.
demis-hassabis.work: Demis Hassabis Thinks We're in the 'Foothills of the Singularity'
demis-hassabis.why: Asked whether government should regulate AI beyond lab self-regulation, he says some form of government involvement and adaptive regulation is required.

ed-zitron.q: we need to start arresting people for committing crimes, halting any and all training runs, and putting real safeguards on this technology
ed-zitron.work: AI Is Already In Dangerous Hands
ed-zitron.why: The author calls for enforced safeguards and criminal accountability for AI labs, which means binding rules rather than self-regulation.

eliezer-yudkowsky.q: Put a ceiling on how much computing power anyone is allowed to use in training an AI system, and move it downward over the coming years to compensate for more efficient training algorithms.
eliezer-yudkowsky.work: The Only Way to Deal With the Threat From AI? Shut It Down
eliezer-yudkowsky.why: He proposes legally binding, internationally enforced compute limits on AI training.

elon-musk.q: I really think we need government regulation here, just to — because. This is insuring the public good is served.
elon-musk.work: Elon Musk Governor's Interview (NGA 2017, AI segment transcript)
elon-musk.why: He calls for government regulation of companies racing to build AI, with regulators able to make them pause until safety is shown.

emily-m-bender.q: Yes, there is an urgent need to address the harm being done by so-called “AI” and to set up effective regulation and governance so that those who are impacted by this technology have power over how it is deployed.
emily-m-bender.work: On NYT Magazine on AI: Resist the Urge to be Impressed
emily-m-bender.why: She calls for effective regulation of the companies building and deploying these systems, such as OpenAI.

gary-marcus.q: We need serious regulation to prevent AI’s from running amok. Voluntary agreements between companies are not going to cut it.
gary-marcus.work: Why my p(doom) has risen, dramatically
gary-marcus.why: The author calls in his own voice for serious regulation beyond voluntary industry agreements.

guillaume-verdon.q: So we’re actually for reliability engineering, we just think that the market is much more efficient at achieving this sort of reliability optimum than sort of heavy-handed regulations that are written by the incumbents
guillaume-verdon.work: Guillaume Verdon: Beff Jezos, E/acc Movement, Physics, Computation & AGI (Lex Fridman Podcast #407)
guillaume-verdon.why: He prefers market selection and deployer liability to regulation of AI developers.

helen-toner.q: First, we should be implementing transparency requirements for developers of high stakes AI systems.
helen-toner.work: Transcript: Senate Judiciary Subcommittee hearing, "Oversight of AI: Insiders' Perspectives"
helen-toner.why: In her own Senate testimony she asks Congress to impose transparency requirements on developers, along with liability rules and whistleblower protections.

holly-elmore.q: Right now, we need to regulate the process of building frontier AI itself.
holly-elmore.why: She closes her essay by calling for regulation of frontier AI development now.

jack-clark.q: we are going to need to work together to create unusual and serious rules for this technology and the companies building it, and to exercise the hardest and I think most noble quality of people - restraint.
jack-clark.work: Import AI 477: In which I tell the IMF the Singularity has begun
jack-clark.why: Speaking to policymakers, the author calls for serious rules on frontier AI companies, and earlier says 'We will also likely need rules to govern this.'

josh-hawley.q: And the government should inspect all of these frontier AI systems, so we can better understand what the tech titans plan to build and deploy.
josh-hawley.why: Among his proposed 'guardrails', he calls for mandatory government inspection of frontier AI systems.

karen-hao.q: But yeah, increasing transparency is a really huge one—just understanding what these companies are feeding into their models, what they're using, what kind of research they're actually doing, and what research they might be censoring internally and not allowing the public to see.
karen-hao.why: Asked what she would do now, she calls for transparency and other laws on AI companies, after saying transparency laws should have existed before the generative AI boom.

leopold-aschenbrenner.q: This will involve invasive restrictions on AI labs and on the core team of AGI researchers, from extreme vetting to constant monitoring to working from a SCIF to reduced freedom to leave
leopold-aschenbrenner.why: In a passage saying 'we obviously need to lock this stuff down', he calls for government-backed mandatory security restrictions on AI labs (while doubting ordinary safety regulation is sufficient).

max-tegmark.q: I never thought governments would let AI companies get this far without any meaningful regulation.
max-tegmark.work: How to Keep AI Under Control
max-tegmark.why: He presents the absence of meaningful government regulation of AI companies as a failure, alongside saying industry cannot self-regulate.

meredith-whittaker.q: It is imperative that lawmakers regulate to ensure that these systems are accountable, accurate, contestable, and that those most at risk of harm have a say in how, and whether, they are used.
meredith-whittaker.work: Written Testimony of Meredith Whittaker: "Artificial Intelligence: Societal and Ethical Implications"
meredith-whittaker.why: In testimony to Congress about systems built by a handful of private AI companies, she calls for binding regulation, not voluntary ethics.

mustafa-suleyman.q: Alongside spelling out very precisely the kind of superintelligence we should build, the time has come to also consider what societal boundaries, norms and laws we want around this process.
mustafa-suleyman.why: He calls for laws around superintelligence development and later says accountability and oversight are to be welcomed.

pope-leo-xiv.q: It is necessary to establish adequate regulatory tools capable of upholding justice and curbing the distorting effects of technological power.
pope-leo-xiv.work: Magnifica Humanitas: Encyclical on safeguarding the human person in the time of Artificial Intelligence
pope-leo-xiv.why: He calls for regulatory tools to curb the power of the private actors driving AI development.

sam-altman.q: The US government, and all other governments, should regulate the development of SMI.
sam-altman.why: He proposes government regulation of SMI development, including observation of companies and required safeguards.

samuel-hammond.q: You can be ambivalent about the usefulness of most forms of AI regulation and still favor oversight of the frontier labs.
samuel-hammond.why: He favors mandatory safety testing and disclosure for frontier labs, while being skeptical of most other AI regulation.

timnit-gebru.q: While those are important, the #1 thing that would safeguard us from unsafe uses of AI is curbing the power of the companies who develop it and increasing the power of those who speak up against the harms of AI and these companies’ practices.
timnit-gebru.work: For truly ethical AI, its research must be independent from big tech
timnit-gebru.why: She calls technology-specific regulations important and says the top safeguard is curbing the power of the companies that develop AI.

yann-lecun.q: The question that people are debating is whether it makes sense to regulate research and development of AI. And I don't think it does.
yann-lecun.work: How Not to Be Stupid About AI, With Yann LeCun
yann-lecun.why: While accepting existing product-safety rules, he rejects regulating AI research and development itself.

yoshua-bengio.q: For example, banning powerful AI systems (say beyond the abilities of GPT-4) that are given autonomy and agency would be a good start. This would entail both national regulation and international agreements.
yoshua-bengio.why: He proposes binding national regulation and treaties restricting the most powerful autonomous AI systems.

zvi-mowshowitz.q: I am most interested in option 4, to require safety cases, even though it is harder to implement.
zvi-mowshowitz.why: On the options for pacing frontier AI, he favors requiring safety cases from developers, which is a binding rule.

alondra-nelson.q: The purpose of AI is not scale or efficiency. The purpose of AI is people.
alondra-nelson.work: Three Fallacies: Alondra Nelson's Remarks at Élysée Palace on the Occasion of the AI Action Summit
alondra-nelson.why: She states in her own voice that people are the purpose AI should serve.

anton-korinek.q: If we want those AIs to be aligned, part of that alignment is to take care of the basic material needs of humans and ideally a little bit more than just the basic needs.
anton-korinek.work: Anton Korinek on Automating Work and the Economics of an Intelligence Explosion
anton-korinek.why: He defines AI alignment as AI serving human wellbeing.

arvind-narayanan.q: If you’re imagining a future where AI is actually owning and running companies and hiring and firing people, that’s already dystopian.
arvind-narayanan.work: What will be left for us to work on?
arvind-narayanan.why: He holds that a future where AI rather than humans runs things is dystopian whatever its alignment, and he calls for humans to stay the 'superintelligences of the future'.

audrey-tang.q: We, the people, are the superintelligence. Let us design AI to serve at the speed of society, and make democracy fast, fair, and fun.
audrey-tang.why: Closing a talk that rejects the singularity and the AI-as-gardener model, she says AI should be designed to serve people and society.

bernie-sanders.q: Humanity must not allow a handful of multibillionaires to recklessly attempt to replace us.
bernie-sanders.work: Don't Let Big Tech Dictate Humanity's Future
bernie-sanders.why: Arguing against transhumanist visions of humans as a step toward superintelligence, he insists humans must not be replaced and that 'Human beings, not machines, must come first.'

e-glen-weyl.q: It is not surprising that quantitative technical and economic arguments converge on the centrality of human value.
e-glen-weyl.work: AI Is an Ideology, Not a Technology
e-glen-weyl.why: In an essay rejecting the ideology that technology should replace much of humanity, the authors affirm human value as central to what technology serves.

emily-m-bender.q: “How do we imagine and deploy design processes that locate technology as tools, shaped for and in the service of people working towards pro-social ends?”
emily-m-bender.work: On NYT Magazine on AI: Resist the Urge to be Impressed
emily-m-bender.why: She offers this as the question that should frame AI, in place of building AI as autonomous agents.

guillaume-verdon.q: if one seeks to increase the amount of intelligence in the universe, staying perpetually anchored to the human form as our prior is counter-productive and overly restrictive/suboptimal
guillaume-verdon.work: Notes on e/acc principles and tenets
guillaume-verdon.why: In a post-humanist passage he rejects keeping the human form as the goal.

helen-toner.q: Analogously, we can say that a world with AI calling the shots and humans either dead or disempowered would not count as real dynamism, even if there were a vibrant AI economy of invention and creation.
helen-toner.work: In search of a dynamist vision for safe superhuman AI
helen-toner.why: She makes human agency a core requirement of a good future and rejects a future where AI runs things and humans are sidelined, however vibrant the AI economy.

holly-elmore.q: Humans minds are the source of truth about what makes us suffer or flourish, and the Singularity futures become dystopias because they have moved beyond the point of groundtruthing with human minds.
holly-elmore.why: She argues human minds must remain the reference for value and that moving beyond humans is what makes Singularity futures dystopian.

jason-crawford.q: Jobs and technology have a purpose: producing the good and services we need to live and thrive.
jason-crawford.work: The future of humanity is in management
jason-crawford.why: He treats technology, including advanced AI, as serving human needs, and envisions humanity as the 'board of directors' setting the goals.

josh-hawley.q: I say again, AI should serve human beings, not the other way around.
josh-hawley.why: In a speech against transhumanism, which he says treats ordinary humanity as something to transcend, he states that AI must serve humans.

marc-andreessen.q: It serves us. The techno-capital machine works for us. All the machines work for us.
marc-andreessen.why: He insists that technology, including the machines, exists to serve human beings.

mark-zuckerberg.q: Meta's vision is to bring personal superintelligence to everyone. We believe in putting this power in people's hands to direct it towards what they value in their own lives.
mark-zuckerberg.why: His essay frames superintelligence as a tool individuals direct toward their own goals, in contrast to AI that replaces large swaths of society.

max-tegmark.q: it’s likely that the resulting superintelligence will not only replace us, but also lack anything resembling human consciousness, compassion or morality – something we’ll view less as our worthy descendants than as an unstoppable plague.
max-tegmark.work: The 'Don't Look Up' Thinking That Could Doom Us With AI
max-tegmark.why: Rebutting the view that AI is 'the natural next stage of cosmic life', he rejects humanity being replaced by AI.

mustafa-suleyman.q: We are not building an ill-defined and ethereal superintelligence; we are building a practical technology explicitly designed only to serve humanity.
mustafa-suleyman.why: His humanist superintelligence essay says AI must serve humanity and keep humans in control.

nick-land.q: Whatever we want (consistently) leads through Pythia. Thus, what we really want, is Pythia.
nick-land.why: Answering a self-described human-supremacist, Land concludes that what we really want is the superior machine intelligence (Pythia), not human-directed ends.

paul-kingsnorth.q: What - or who - do they ultimately serve? Humanity or the Machine? Nature or the technium? God or His adversary?
paul-kingsnorth.why: His test for any technology is whether it serves humanity rather than the Machine, and throughout he opposes the posthuman project of surpassing human beings.

pope-leo-xiv.q: For this reason, humanity — in all its grandeur and woundedness — must never be replaced or surpassed.
pope-leo-xiv.work: Magnifica Humanitas: Encyclical on safeguarding the human person in the time of Artificial Intelligence
pope-leo-xiv.why: He states directly that humanity must never be replaced or surpassed by technological progress.

venkatesh-rao.q: The desirable future of AI is not permanent human supremacy over increasingly capable artificial “servants.”
venkatesh-rao.why: Against Microsoft's 'AI serves people' humanism, he argues for a symbiotic future and rejects any special human essence that AI should serve.

vitalik-buterin.q: It seems very hard to have a "friendly" superintelligent-AI-dominated world where humans are anything other than pets.
vitalik-buterin.why: Under the heading 'The world I don't want to see', he rejects futures in which superintelligent AI surpasses and sidelines humans.

yann-lecun.q: The point is, AI systems, as smart as they might be, will be subservient to us. We set their goals, and they don't have any intrinsic goal that we would build into them to dominate.
yann-lecun.work: Meta's AI Chief Yann LeCun on AGI, Open-Source, and AI Risk
yann-lecun.why: He frames AI as systems built to serve human-set goals, never to dominate humans.

alondra-nelson.q: Thoughtful regulation catalyzes the development and adoption of new technologies, ensuring that no tradeoff between safety and progress or rights and innovation is necessary.
alondra-nelson.work: Regulating AI in the Evolving Transatlantic Landscape
alondra-nelson.why: She denies that regulation trades off against innovation, saying it speeds development, which negates the claim that regulation would deter innovation.

bernie-sanders.q: That is why I have introduced legislation to impose a federal moratorium on the construction of new AI data centers until strong safeguards are enacted.
bernie-sanders.work: Artificial intelligence is coming for the working class. We must fight back
bernie-sanders.why: He proposes strict measures now, a federal moratorium until strong safeguards exist, so he does not think strict regulation does more harm than good.

daniel-kokotajlo.q: I think that the US government should intervene.
daniel-kokotajlo.why: He asks the government to step in and pace the frontier so that progress toward AI research automation bends downward, which means he does not see slowing innovation as a net harm.

david-sacks.q: Although we want a light touch on AI regulations, President Trump made clear that we do not intend to ignore the risks of this revolutionary technological power. We can monitor risks, and secure our edge, without stifling innovation.
david-sacks.work: Thread on the White House AI Action Plan and Trump's first major AI speech
david-sacks.why: In his own framing of the Action Plan, he favors light-touch AI regulation to avoid stifling innovation.

dean-ball.q: Here is what this means in practice: I oppose literally almost all AI regulation.
dean-ball.work: Before Leviathan Wakes (Why I Believe What I Believe)
dean-ball.why: He opposes nearly all AI regulation and wants to deregulate so that AI 'can transform our lives'; the one exception he names is narrow catastrophic-risk management.

ed-zitron.q: If LLMs were a toy, they’d be taken off the shelves. If LLMs were a drug, they would be banned.
ed-zitron.work: AI Is Already In Dangerous Hands
ed-zitron.why: The author says LLMs deserve product-safety-level restriction or bans, which contradicts the view that strict regulation would do more harm than good.

eliezer-yudkowsky.q: Shut down all the large GPU clusters (the large computer farms where the most powerful AIs are refined). Shut down all the large training runs.
eliezer-yudkowsky.work: The Only Way to Deal With the Threat From AI? Shut It Down
eliezer-yudkowsky.why: He demands the strictest possible restrictions now, the opposite of holding that strict regulation would do more harm than good.

gary-marcus.q: The Information’s oped complains that “California’s effort to regulate AI would stifle innovation”, but never really details how.
gary-marcus.work: The misguided backlash against California's SB-1047
gary-marcus.why: In defending SB-1047 (and urging it be made stronger), he dismisses the claim that the regulation would stifle innovation.

guillaume-verdon.q: over-regulating technologies suppresses variance and hence slows down progress towards higher utility technologies and advancement of civilization, a contrast to anti-AGI factions of EA
guillaume-verdon.work: Notes on e/acc principles and tenets
guillaume-verdon.why: He argues regulation slows technological progress.

holly-elmore.q: Properly governing the attempt to build frontier AI is the only way we will ever have an AGI safe enough to coexist with us, let alone a superintelligence that can safely exceed us in any unsupervised capacity.
holly-elmore.why: She holds that governing frontier AI development now is necessary, the opposite of saying strict regulation would do more harm than good.

jason-crawford.q: This could end up like nuclear, where nothing gets approved and progress stalls for decades.
jason-crawford.work: A plea for solutionism on AI safety
jason-crawford.why: Of a new agency demanding proof of safety before approving AI systems, he warns it could stall progress for decades, preferring an incremental approach like the DOT's for self-driving cars; he still supports safety work.

jd-vance.q: But it will never come to pass if overregulation deters innovators from taking the risks necessary to advance the ball, nor will it occur if we allow AI to become dominated by massive players looking to use the tech to censor or control users' thoughts.
jd-vance.work: Remarks by the Vice President at the Artificial Intelligence Action Summit in Paris, France
jd-vance.why: He argues that heavy AI regulation now would deter innovation and block the coming industrial revolution.

karen-hao.q: And I think we would have just a fundamentally different trajectory for AI as well, because the AI industry could have only manifested the way that it did on the backs of sloppy legislation and regulation.
karen-hao.why: She blames weak regulation for the industry's harms and wishes stronger laws had been in place.

marc-andreessen.q: For AI risk, these are CEOs who stand to make more money if regulatory barriers are erected that form a cartel of government-blessed AI vendors protected from new startup and open source competition – the software version of “too big to fail” banks.
marc-andreessen.work: Why AI Will Save the World
marc-andreessen.why: In arguing that the drive for AI regulation is being captured by 'Bootleggers', he holds that new AI rules would entrench incumbents and shut out startup and open-source innovation.

meredith-whittaker.q: Congress has a window to act, and the time is now. Powerful AI systems are currently reshaping our lives and social institutions in ways that we aren't able to measure or contest.
meredith-whittaker.work: Written Testimony of Meredith Whittaker: "Artificial Intelligence: Societal and Ethical Implications"
meredith-whittaker.why: She urges Congress to regulate AI now, and elsewhere she dismisses arguments that guardrails would make the US lose ground, so she rejects the claim that strict regulation now would do more harm.

pope-leo-xiv.q: Indeed, these criteria do not constitute a curb on innovation; instead they make it civilized and humane.
pope-leo-xiv.work: Magnifica Humanitas: Encyclical on safeguarding the human person in the time of Artificial Intelligence
pope-leo-xiv.why: After listing oversight, accountability and equity measures, he denies that they hold back innovation.

robin-hanson.q: In fact, progress seems to me to be slowing down worldwide due to excess fear-induced regulation.
robin-hanson.why: Arguing against regulating to slow AI, he says fear-induced regulation has stopped progress on other technologies.

timnit-gebru.q: Contrary to big tech executives’ cold-war style rhetoric about an arms race, what truly stifles innovation is the current arrangement where a few people build harmful technology and others constantly work to prevent harm
timnit-gebru.work: For truly ethical AI, its research must be independent from big tech
timnit-gebru.why: She rejects the claim that constraints stifle innovation, locating the real drag on innovation in the concentrated power of big tech.

yoshua-bengio.q: However, from the point of view of ordinary citizens and of public policy, the prudent approach into AGI is clearly preferable when adding up the risks and benefits.
yoshua-bengio.work: Reasoning through arguments against taking AI safety seriously
yoshua-bengio.why: Answering the accelerationist case that slowing AI forfeits benefits, he concludes the cautious, regulated path is better on balance.

zvi-mowshowitz.q: This leads to the standard (and usually highly accurate) objections that regulations never work out the way you want them to and always stifle innovation and progress. Except, here, that could be exactly what we need to protect against existential risk
zvi-mowshowitz.work: On the FLI AI-Risk Open Letter
zvi-mowshowitz.why: He grants that regulation usually stifles innovation, but argues that for AI that slowing may be exactly what is needed.

andrej-karpathy.q: With AI we’re going to see the exact same thing. It’s just more automation.
andrej-karpathy.work: Andrej Karpathy: AGI is still a decade away
andrej-karpathy.why: After noting that computers and mobile phones never showed up as a break in GDP, he predicts AI will follow the same pattern, which uses earlier general-purpose technologies as the guide (though his 'Power to the people' essay notes that LLM diffusion reverses the usual top-down pattern).

anton-korinek.q: But the fundamental difference is that there were always things that only humans could do. And that will no longer be true if we have a AGI.
anton-korinek.work: #14: Anton Korinek on AI's Economic and Workforce Impacts (transcript)
anton-korinek.why: Against the economics profession's reliance on past automation, he argues AGI breaks the historical pattern.

arvind-narayanan.q: It is guided by lessons from past technological revolutions, such as the slow and uncertain nature of technology adoption and diffusion.
arvind-narayanan.why: Their framework explicitly takes past general-purpose technologies as the guide to how AI will diffuse and affect society.

brian-merchant.q: If we are to truly understand the impacts of mass automation technologies like AI, and why there’s a vociferous and fast-growing backlash to it, then it’s crucial that we rethink our dismissal of the Luddites.
brian-merchant.work: Understanding the Luddites in the age of AI
brian-merchant.why: He argues the history of Industrial Revolution automation is the key guide to AI's impacts and the public reaction to it.

daron-acemoglu.q: And I kept saying no, no, I'm saying this time is the same, but it seemed like people had a too rosy a picture of what happened in the past, so that's part of the reason why a lot of the book is dedicated to history.
daron-acemoglu.work: Mindscape 283: Daron Acemoglu on Technology, Inequality, and Power
daron-acemoglu.why: He explicitly treats the history of earlier technologies, such as the Industrial Revolution, as the guide to how AI will play out.

dean-ball.q: I cannot tell you whether the dynamism that results will be fundamentally good or fundamentally bad, though history tells me it will be good.
dean-ball.why: He uses the record of past technology to judge how AI will turn out; elsewhere he calls AI a general-purpose technology that follows the overall pattern of earlier ones.

elon-musk.q: So the future is going to be very, very different from the past. There’s no analogy or metaphor that I think illustrates the magnitude of change that we’re going to experience here.
elon-musk.work: Full Transcript: Zanny Minton Beddoes Interviews Elon Musk (The Economist)
elon-musk.why: He says no past analogy captures the change AI and robots will bring, denying that history is a good guide here.

jack-clark.q: discuss why, if the technology advances as much as I think, that AI cannot be treated as a normal technology.
jack-clark.work: Import AI 458: Reckoning with the future; and a singularity story
jack-clark.why: The author's thesis is that AI cannot be treated as a normal technology, and later he says self-improving AI is a class of technology that 'has never existed before'.

jason-crawford.q: But short of that, I expect that AI will do what all fundamental enabling general-purpose technologies have done throughout all of human history: raise our standard of living and accelerate progress.
jason-crawford.work: The future of humanity is in management
jason-crawford.why: He explicitly uses earlier general-purpose technologies as the guide to AI's effects, while also rebutting 'this time it's different' arguments.

jd-vance.q: Now, in the 1970s, if you go back a little ways, many feared that the automated teller machine -- what we call the "ATM" -- would replace bank tellers. In reality, the advent of the ATM made bank tellers more productive
jd-vance.work: Remarks by the Vice President at the American Dynamism Summit
jd-vance.why: He uses the history of earlier automation, like the ATM, as a guide to how AI will affect jobs.

marc-andreessen.q: Historically, every new technology that matters, from electric lighting to automobiles to radio to the Internet, has sparked a moral panic – a social contagion that convinces people the new technology is going to destroy the world, or society, or both.
marc-andreessen.work: Why AI Will Save the World
marc-andreessen.why: He uses the history of earlier technologies' reception as the template for understanding the current reaction to AI.

mark-zuckerberg.q: The common belief is that AI will automate jobs away. But that hasn't really been how the history of technology has worked. Usually, you create things that take away 90% of the work, and that leads you to want more people, not less.
mark-zuckerberg.work: Mark Zuckerberg: AI will write most Meta code in 18 months
mark-zuckerberg.why: He uses the history of technology, plus the truck-driving example just before, as his guide to what AI will do to jobs.

max-tegmark.q: And if you think of AI, if you think of superintelligence in particular, as just another technology, like electricity, you're probably not very worried.
max-tegmark.work: How to Keep AI Under Control
max-tegmark.why: He argues that treating superintelligence like electricity is the mistake that leads people to underrate it.

mustafa-suleyman.q: AI is to the mind what nuclear fusion is to energy. Limitless, abundant, world-changing. And AI really is different, and that means we have to think about it creatively and honestly.
mustafa-suleyman.why: He calls the 'just another general-purpose technology like printing or steam' answer defensive and argues AI is different from any earlier invention.

noah-smith.q: But when we think about the technologies now being invented, we often forget this lesson — or at least, many of us do.
noah-smith.work: I love AI. Why doesn't everyone?
noah-smith.why: Right after saying past technologies made things better, he says the same lesson should be applied to new technologies like AI, and the essay goes on to compare how AI is received with how earlier technologies were.

robin-hanson.q: You might think that folks would take a lesson from our history of prior bursts of anxiety and concern about automation, bursts which have appeared roughly every three decades since at least the 1930s.
robin-hanson.why: He uses history of past technologies and automation scares as the guide to AI, against the 'foom' scenario.

samuel-hammond.q: The reference class of prior technological transitions (agricultural revolution, printing press, industrialization) all feature regime changes to varying degrees.
samuel-hammond.why: He explicitly uses prior technological transitions as the reference class for what AI will do, and builds his Leviathan essays on the printing-press analogy.

tyler-cowen.q: It's going to be a tough slog, like the printing press, like electricity. The people who study diffusion of new technologies never think there will be rapid takeoff.
tyler-cowen.work: Tyler Cowen — The #1 bottleneck to AI progress is humans
tyler-cowen.why: He uses earlier general-purpose technologies as the guide to how AI will spread.

vitalik-buterin.q: The class of things in that category is much smaller: we might plausibly include humans surpassing monkeys, multicellular life surpassing unicellular life, the origin of life itself, and perhaps the Industrial Revolution, in which machine edged out man in physical strength.
vitalik-buterin.why: He argues AI belongs not with past technologies like the printing press but with far rarer transitions, so earlier technologies are a poor guide ('walking on much less well-trodden ground').

yann-lecun.q: But people are exploiting the fear about the technology, and we’re running the risk of scaring people away from it. That's a mistake we made with other technologies that revolutionized the world. Take the invention of the printing press in the 15th century.
yann-lecun.work: How Not to Be Stupid About AI, With Yann LeCun
yann-lecun.why: He uses the reception of the printing press as a guide to how AI is being received.

anton-korinek.q: But I think now we are so close. We are just a couple years from it, and the research is suddenly extremely urgent and relevant in much shorter time scales.
anton-korinek.work: Transcript of Anton Korinek on What Happens When AI Replaces Every Job?
anton-korinek.why: He treats AGI that surpasses humans across the board as only a couple of years away, which is the opposite of calling the promises hype.

arvind-narayanan.q: Unfortunately, instead of admitting they were wrong about their naive “AGI in 3 years” predictions, they've decided to save face by watering down what they mean by AGI so much that it's meaningless now.
arvind-narayanan.why: In an essay calling scaling-to-AGI claims myths, the authors describe AI leaders' public AGI promises as naive and wrong.

bernie-sanders.q: Artificial intelligence (AI) is the most transformational technology in the history of the world — and will have a profound impact on the life of every man, woman and child in our country.
bernie-sanders.work: Artificial intelligence is coming for the working class. We must fight back
bernie-sanders.why: He takes AI's transformative claims at face value rather than as hype.

brian-merchant.q: Now, it needs to be underlined once again that generative AI is not yet the one-size-fits-all agent of job replacement its salesmen would like it to be—far from it.
brian-merchant.work: The AI jobs crisis is here, now
brian-merchant.why: He says the sales claims for generative AI far exceed its capabilities, a theme repeated in his GPT-5 piece calling the launch a failure on its own hyped terms.

daniel-kokotajlo.q: Many people seem to be dismissing this hypothesis ‘on priors’ because it sounds crazy. But actually, a reasonable prior should conclude that this is plausible.
daniel-kokotajlo.work: Training AGI in Secret would be Unsafe and Unethical
daniel-kokotajlo.why: He argues that the claim that AGI will arrive this decade is plausible, not hype to be dismissed.

dario-amodei.q: but the truth is that behind the volatility and public speculation, there has been a smooth, unyielding increase in AI’s cognitive capabilities.
dario-amodei.why: He rejects the view that AI progress is hitting a wall and says capabilities are rising steadily, with powerful AI possibly a few years away.

dean-ball.q: These debates have largely been settled by empirical reality, and it is long past time to move on and accept the enormity of what is unfolding at the frontiers of AI.
dean-ball.why: He says the doubts about AI capabilities have been settled by reality and asks readers to accept how large the change is, which rejects the view that the promises are mostly hype.

demis-hassabis.q: I sometimes describe it, quantify it as 10 times the impact the Industrial Revolution was, 10 times faster.
demis-hassabis.work: Demis Hassabis Thinks We're in the 'Foothills of the Singularity'
demis-hassabis.why: He says the technology's impact will be enormous (and calls this probably an underestimate), the opposite of calling the promises hype.

ed-zitron.q: I believe that the generative AI market is a $50 billion revenue industry masquerading as a $1 trillion one, and the media is helping.
ed-zitron.work: The Hater's Guide To The AI Bubble
ed-zitron.why: In a section titled 'AI Is Predominantly Marketed Based On Lies', the author says the industry's claimed scale is a pretence amplified by the media.

emily-m-bender.q: The division of labor between those who construct datasets and those who build the algorithms sets the conditions for wild over-claims about system capabilities.
emily-m-bender.work: Resisting Dehumanization in the Age of "AI"
emily-m-bender.why: Across her texts she treats claims about AI capabilities as hype to be deflated; here she names wild over-claims as structural.

gary-marcus.q: The failure of the AI 2027 team to reckon with the immense history of broken promises and delays in the AI field is, in a team that styles itself as forecasters, inexcusable.
gary-marcus.work: The 'AI 2027' Scenario: How realistic is it?
gary-marcus.why: He characterises the AI field's public predictions as a long history of broken promises, alongside examples like hallucinations and driverless cars.

geoffrey-hinton.q: What's going to happen when they get smarter than us? Because they are going to get smarter than us.
geoffrey-hinton.work: Will AI outsmart human intelligence? (Royal Institution lecture, transcript)
geoffrey-hinton.why: He treats claims of rapidly growing AI capability as real, rejecting the 'just autocomplete' dismissal.

helen-toner.q: Dismissing discussion of AGI, human-level AI, transformative AI, superintelligence, etc. as “science fiction” should be seen as a sign of total unseriousness.
helen-toner.work: "Long" timelines to advanced AI have gotten crazy short
helen-toner.why: In a post arguing that even skeptical experts now expect human-level AI within a decade or two, she rejects writing off claims about advanced AI as fantasy.

jack-clark.q: What I am here to explain today is that AI is on a course to bring about even more change than what we are expecting and we should prepare accordingly.
jack-clark.work: Import AI 477: In which I tell the IMF the Singularity has begun
jack-clark.why: The author argues that current expectations understate AI's impact, the opposite of calling the promises inflated hype.

jason-crawford.q: It is now impossible not to see that this is going to change the world, indeed that the change has already begun and is underway in earnest.
jason-crawford.why: After describing his own experience with coding agents, he says AI's transformative effect is real and already happening.

jd-vance.q: Now, our administration -- the Trump Administration -- believes that AI will have countless, revolutionary applications in economic inv- -- innovation, job creation, national security, health care, free expression, and beyond.
jd-vance.work: Remarks by the Vice President at the Artificial Intelligence Action Summit in Paris, France
jd-vance.why: He affirms that AI's promised revolutionary benefits are real, not hype.

karen-hao.q: There is a vagueness about it, a purposeful vagueness about it I think in the way that Altman uses it and used it in reference to the way that the tech industry evokes this hand wavy idea that there will be more for everyone.
karen-hao.work: Decolonizing the Future: Karen Hao on Resisting the Empire of AI
karen-hao.why: She describes industry promises of AI abundance as purposefully vague rhetoric that masks the opposite outcome.

leopold-aschenbrenner.q: Even now, barely anyone is pricing all this in. But situational awareness on AI isn’t actually that hard, once you step back and look at the trends.
leopold-aschenbrenner.work: I. From GPT-4 to AGI: Counting the OOMs
leopold-aschenbrenner.why: He argues that expectations about AI are too low, not inflated, and that trendlines support AGI by 2027.

marc-andreessen.q: AI is quite possibly the most important – and best – thing our civilization has ever created, certainly on par with electricity and microchips, and probably beyond those.
marc-andreessen.work: Why AI Will Save the World
marc-andreessen.why: He treats the large promises of AI as genuine, calling it possibly the most important and best thing civilization has created.

mark-zuckerberg.q: Over the last few months we have begun to see glimpses of our AI systems improving themselves. The improvement is slow for now, but undeniable. Developing superintelligence is now in sight.
mark-zuckerberg.why: He asserts as his own view that self-improvement is undeniable and superintelligence is in sight, the opposite of calling such promises mostly hype.

max-tegmark.q: I know some skeptics are saying, "Nah, they're just overhyped stochastic parrots that lack a model of the world," but they clearly have a representation of the world.
max-tegmark.work: How to Keep AI Under Control
max-tegmark.why: He rebuts the claim that language models are overhyped, after saying AI progress went faster than he predicted.

meredith-whittaker.q: So I don't, you know, I'm not saying it's useless.  I'm saying it is vastly overhyped.
meredith-whittaker.work: Signal's President on AI, Advertising, and Running a Popular Messaging App
meredith-whittaker.why: Asked about generative AI, she says directly that it is vastly overhyped and that the claims made about it are disconnected from reality.

mustafa-suleyman.q: We will see the arrival of medical superintelligence in the next few years.
mustafa-suleyman.why: He makes and stands behind strong near-term capability claims, pointing to his lab's diagnostic results as evidence.

noah-smith.q: If anything it understates the pace and magnitude of the changes taking place.
noah-smith.work: You are no longer the smartest type of thing on Earth
noah-smith.why: On a viral article about AI's rapid progress, he says that if anything it understates the change, the opposite of calling the claims hype.

sam-altman.q: There are a lot of details we still have to figure out, but it’s a mistake to get distracted by any particular challenge. Deep learning works, and we will solve the remaining problems.
sam-altman.why: He affirms that AI's promised capabilities are real and will be delivered.

samuel-hammond.q: The last 12 months of AI progress were the slowest they’ll be for the foreseeable future.
samuel-hammond.why: Under the heading 'AI progress is accelerating, not plateauing', he holds that AI's capabilities will grow fast, not that the claims are hype.

timnit-gebru.q: Far from the sophisticated, sentient machines portrayed in media and pop culture, so-called AI systems are fueled by millions of underpaid workers around the world, performing repetitive tasks under precarious labor conditions.
timnit-gebru.work: The Exploited Labor Behind Artificial Intelligence
timnit-gebru.why: She presents the public picture of sophisticated AI as inflated, calling the systems 'so-called AI' propped up by hidden human labor.

tyler-cowen.q: Economists, social scientists, most of them are blind and asleep to the promise of strong AI. They're just out to lunch. I think they're wrong. I trust the AI experts.
tyler-cowen.work: Tyler Cowen — The #1 bottleneck to AI progress is humans
tyler-cowen.why: While expecting slow diffusion, he says the promise of strong AI is real and underrated.

william-macaskill.q: It seems likely to us that AI research effort will reach parity with human research labour within the next two decades, meaning AI systems can collectively perform almost all the research-relevant cognitive work that humans can.
william-macaskill.why: He forecasts transformative AI capability on short timelines, the opposite of treating AI promises as mostly hype.

zvi-mowshowitz.q: Even if AI could permanently only do the things it can currently do, that would be Internet big, and radically change the world, mostly for the better.
zvi-mowshowitz.why: He argues that even current AI is underrated and that capabilities will go much further, the opposite of calling the promises hype.

anton-korinek.q: So we only need to compensate workers in scenarios where growth would also be significantly higher. And I think that would make it affordable to pay out the UBI that makes sure that workers are not worse off materially.
anton-korinek.work: Anton Korinek on Automating Work and the Economics of an Intelligence Explosion
anton-korinek.why: He backs a seed universal basic income that can scale up as a way to share AGI's gains with displaced workers.

josh-hawley.q: A republic of free citizens cannot be built on a check.
josh-hawley.work: The American Covenant’s Answer to AI
josh-hawley.why: Responding to universal basic income for displaced workers, he calls it 'a hollow answer' and says paying people not to work degrades them.

marc-andreessen.q: We believe a Universal Basic Income would turn people into zoo animals to be farmed by the state.
marc-andreessen.why: He explicitly rejects a universal basic income, the paradigm case of direct distribution to citizens.

sam-altman.q: We should therefore focus on taxing capital rather than labor, and we should use these taxes as an opportunity to directly distribute ownership and wealth to citizens.
sam-altman.why: He proposes directly distributing ownership and wealth to citizens through an American Equity Fund.

anton-korinek.q: And what I anticipate is that our current system of income distribution, which revolves largely about people receiving most of their income from work or from having worked in the past and receiving a pension, it’s just not going to work that way anymore after we have AGI
anton-korinek.work: Transcript of Anton Korinek on What Happens When AI Replaces Every Job?
anton-korinek.why: Asked how to stop AI gains going only to a few, he says the current work-based distribution system will fail and must be rethought.

bernie-sanders.q: Replacing workers with revolutionary new technology is a good investment for billionaires. But for the working class of this country, AI and robotics could well be a nightmare.
bernie-sanders.work: Artificial intelligence is coming for the working class. We must fight back
bernie-sanders.why: He argues that without new policy (shorter workweeks, a new social contract) AI-driven productivity will harm most workers.

brian-merchant.q: We do know that it will be used to surveil workers, speed-up work, and be used as leverage against them. That’s already happening, right now.
brian-merchant.work: Understanding the Luddites in the age of AI
brian-merchant.why: Drawing on the Luddite history of automation depressing wages, he says AI is already being used against workers and calls for labor law, collective bargaining and democratic checks.

curtis-yarvin.q: LLMs are incredibly cool and useful tools and will have a huge impact on society. Probably mostly for the worse, since tech is the resource curse, the curse of an economy with inadequate labor demand.
curtis-yarvin.why: He predicts LLM productivity will make most workers useless, like an oil economy, rather than leave them better off.

daron-acemoglu.q: So that's why I don't think we can say, oh, just let the market reap and after a while things are gonna get better. So you have to have a sort of proactive agenda of how can we fix this?
daron-acemoglu.work: Mindscape 283: Daron Acemoglu on Technology, Inequality, and Power
daron-acemoglu.why: After describing 90 years of stagnant worker wages in the British Industrial Revolution, he rejects waiting for markets to deliver gains and calls for institutional and policy action.

e-glen-weyl.q: Yet they have largely been unmatched by the emergence of appropriate labor market institutions (such as unions and labor regulations) that allow workers to share in the potential benefits of these arrangements. Thus, they have tended to raise workplace precarity
e-glen-weyl.why: The authors argue that without new labor institutions and regulation, technology-enabled gains have raised worker precarity rather than leaving workers better off.

jason-crawford.q: If capital increases instead of labor, then wages rise—that’s what has been happening throughout the entire industrial era.
jason-crawford.work: The future of humanity is in management
jason-crawford.why: Rebutting the 'AI drives wages below subsistence' argument, he expects AI-as-capital to raise wages through ordinary economic mechanisms, as industrial technology did.

josh-hawley.q: We must regulate artificial intelligence to ensure that it aids the worker and does not replace him.
josh-hawley.work: The American Covenant’s Answer to AI
josh-hawley.why: He argues that without new policy AI will replace workers and enrich a few, so regulation is needed to make it benefit workers.

marc-andreessen.q: We believe a market sets wages as a function of the marginal productivity of the worker. Therefore technology – which raises productivity – drives wages up, not down.
marc-andreessen.why: He asserts that market wage-setting alone makes productivity-raising technology lift wages, with no policy change required.

paul-kingsnorth.q: Over that time, the Machine has destroyed more livelihoods and lifeways than we could count, from handloom weavers to farmers.
paul-kingsnorth.why: He describes industrial and now AI-driven productivity as destroying workers' livelihoods, adding that 'capitalism has no mercy'.

pope-leo-xiv.q: In this context, without bold decisions, the prospect of greater poverty and inequality looms large, which would leave many individuals marginalized, stranded and surrounded by the machines and automated systems that have replaced them.
pope-leo-xiv.work: Magnifica Humanitas: Encyclical on safeguarding the human person in the time of Artificial Intelligence
pope-leo-xiv.why: He warns that without new policy and protections, AI-driven change threatens to leave many workers poorer.

sam-altman.q: If public policy doesn’t adapt accordingly, most people will end up worse off than they are today.
sam-altman.why: He states that without policy change, AI-driven shifts from labor to capital will leave most people worse off.

arvind-narayanan.q: But it is in contrast to both utopian and dystopian visions of the future of AI which have a common tendency to treat it akin to a separate species, a highly autonomous, potentially superintelligent entity.
arvind-narayanan.why: The normal-technology frame is set explicitly against treating AI as a separate species or autonomous entity, in favour of treating it as a technology like electricity.

balaji-srinivasan.q: AI is amplified intelligence, not artificial intelligence. Today’s AI is not truly agentic because it’s not truly independent of you.
balaji-srinivasan.why: He frames AI as an amplifier of the human user, a tool that depends on you, rather than an independent mind.

brian-merchant.q: we recognize that AI is not sentient, that it’s management, not AI, that fires people
brian-merchant.work: AI Killed My Job: Tech workers
brian-merchant.why: In his own introduction he states AI is not sentient and treats it as a tool managers use, elsewhere calling AI 'a tool for bosses to automate labor'.

curtis-yarvin.q: An LLM as we know it is a tool for humans to use.
curtis-yarvin.why: He argues LLMs are not AI and should be understood as tools, warning against anthropomorphizing them.

daron-acemoglu.q: So if you think of AI as an informational tool, not as something that can write Shakespearean sonnets or pretend to be human.
daron-acemoglu.work: Mindscape 283: Daron Acemoglu on Technology, Inequality, and Power
daron-acemoglu.why: Acemoglu explicitly frames AI as an informational tool rather than something human-like, and elsewhere in the same interview says LLMs lack creativity, wisdom and judgment.

dwarkesh-patel.q: So it becomes hard for us to imagine what it would be like to have a different type of mind come online, and how strange and destructive its methods for executing our commands might be.
dwarkesh-patel.why: Arguing against Andreessen's 'it's just code' view, he describes advanced AI as a different type of mind coming online.

e-glen-weyl.q: If a program is able to distinguish cats from dogs, don’t talk about how a machine is learning to see. Instead talk about how people contributed examples in order to define the visual qualities distinguishing “cats” from “dogs” in a rigorous way for the first time.
e-glen-weyl.work: AI Is an Ideology, Not a Technology
e-glen-weyl.why: The author urges describing AI systems as people collaborating through software rather than as machines that see or think, rejecting the mind framing.

ed-zitron.q: LLMs are cloud software. Framing them as anything else only seeks to mystify them and make the companies seem more powerful, all while doing absolutely nothing to make the world safer or more secure.
ed-zitron.work: AI Is Already In Dangerous Hands
ed-zitron.why: The author says LLMs are ordinary software and that describing them as something more, such as a new lifeform, is mystification.

emily-m-bender.q: Software systems are artifacts, not sentient entities, and as such “teaching” is a misplaced and misleading metaphor (as is “machine learning” or “artificial intelligence”).
emily-m-bender.work: On NYT Magazine on AI: Resist the Urge to be Impressed
emily-m-bender.why: She states plainly that AI systems are artifacts, not minds.

geoffrey-hinton.q: So the point here is they're very like us. They're very unlike computer software.
geoffrey-hinton.work: Will AI outsmart human intelligence? (Royal Institution lecture, transcript)
geoffrey-hinton.why: He argues that large language models understand in the same way humans do and are unlike ordinary software, calling them 'digital beings' elsewhere.

guillaume-verdon.q: Technocapital can usher in the next evolution of consciousness, creating unthinkable next-generation lifeforms and silicon-based awareness.
guillaume-verdon.why: He describes advanced AI as new lifeforms and silicon-based awareness, not mere tools.

jack-clark.q: But make no mistake: what we are dealing with is a real and mysterious creature, not a simple and predictable machine.
jack-clark.work: Import AI 431: Technological Optimism and Appropriate Fear
jack-clark.why: The author explicitly contrasts AI as a 'creature' with the view that it is 'just a tool', and argues for the creature view.

jason-crawford.q: AI is a new kind of tool that we use to get work done, amplifying human productivity.
