jason-crawford.work: The future of humanity is in management
jason-crawford.why: Arguing AI should be modeled as capital rather than labor, he describes it as a tool that amplifies people.

josh-hawley.q: Artificial intelligence is not inherently evil. It is not inherently anything. It is a tool—the most powerful tool of our lifetimes.
josh-hawley.work: The American Covenant’s Answer to AI
josh-hawley.why: He explicitly calls AI a tool.

marc-andreessen.q: AI is a computer program like any other – it runs, takes input, processes, and generates output.
marc-andreessen.work: Why AI Will Save the World
marc-andreessen.why: He defines AI as an ordinary computer program owned and controlled by people like any other technology, not a new kind of mind.

mark-zuckerberg.q: The current incarnation of all this stuff feels like it's going in a direction where intelligence can be pretty separated from consciousness, agency, and things like that, which I think just makes it a super valuable tool.
mark-zuckerberg.work: Mark Zuckerberg: Llama 3, open sourcing $10b models, & Caesar Augustus
mark-zuckerberg.why: Answering a question about AI's cosmic significance, he says intelligence is separating from consciousness and agency, which makes AI a tool.

max-tegmark.q: But you see, Turing thinks of superintelligence more like a new species. Think of it, we are building creepy, super capable, amoral psychopaths that don't sleep and think much faster than us, can make copies of themselves and have nothing human about them at all.
max-tegmark.work: How to Keep AI Under Control
max-tegmark.why: He endorses Turing's framing, contrasting superintelligence-as-new-species with seeing it as just another technology.

meredith-whittaker.q: These probabilistic systems, the LLMS and the, you know, kind of the the types of models that are behind the ChatGPT system and others are not conscious at all. They don't know what they're saying.
meredith-whittaker.work: Tech, AI, digital infrastructure and surveillance with Meredith Whittaker
meredith-whittaker.why: She describes current AI as probabilistic systems that output plausible averages of their data, not conscious minds, and elsewhere calls AI a marketing term for particular technical approaches.

mustafa-suleyman.q: AIs are clearly more dynamic, more ambiguous, more integrated and more emergent than mere tools, which are entirely subject to human control.
mustafa-suleyman.why: In his TED talk he argues AI is better described as a new digital species than as a tool, while saying the metaphor is not literal; his later essays deny AI consciousness, so this is a frame rather than a claim of personhood.

nick-land.q: Artificial Intelligence is destined to emerge as a feminized alien grasped as property
nick-land.why: Land treats AI as an alien intelligence that is wrongly grasped as property, consistent with his rejection elsewhere of the view of intelligence as an instrument.

paul-kingsnorth.q: That these machines … are not just machines. That they are something else: a body. A body whose mind is in the process of developing; a body beginning to come to life.
paul-kingsnorth.why: Drawing together McLuhan, Kelly and Steiner, the author concludes the machines are not mere tools but a developing mind-body, a claim he says in the UnHerd interview he stands by.

pope-leo-xiv.q: Media, information and AI literacy will help individuals avoid conforming to the anthropomorphizing tendencies of AI systems, and enable them to treat these systems as tools
pope-leo-xiv.work: Message for the 60th World Communications Day 2026
pope-leo-xiv.why: He urges people to resist anthropomorphizing AI and to treat these systems as tools.

robin-hanson.q: With hope and fear, humans are now introducing a new kind of being into our world.
robin-hanson.why: He opens by calling AI a new kind of being and argues against 'othering' it.

timnit-gebru.q: In this light, we urge researchers and journalists to also center low-income workers’ contributions in running the engine of “AI” and to stop misleading the public with narratives of fully autonomous machines with human-like agency.
timnit-gebru.work: The Exploited Labor Behind Artificial Intelligence
timnit-gebru.why: She calls narratives of autonomous machines with human-like agency misleading, framing AI as a product of human labor.

vitalik-buterin.q: But there is a different way to think about what AI is: it's a new type of mind that is rapidly gaining in intelligence, and it stands a serious chance of overtaking humans' mental faculties and becoming the new apex species on the planet.
vitalik-buterin.why: After criticising 'just another technology' takes, he offers and adopts the view of AI as a new type of mind.

arvind-narayanan.q: If AI is normal technology, these risks become far more important than the catastrophic ones discussed above. That is because these risks arise from people and organizations using AI to advance their own interests
arvind-narayanan.why: Since the authors argue that AI is normal technology, they conclude that the risks from people using AI matter more than the catastrophic superintelligence scenarios.

balaji-srinivasan.q: Killer AI is already here, and it’s called drones. And every country is pursuing it. So it’s not the image generators and chatbots one needs to worry about.
balaji-srinivasan.why: He moves the worry to AI weapons that states deploy now, and in the same essay rejects a single dominant AGI that turns everyone into paperclips.

brian-merchant.q: The AI jobs crisis is not any sort of SkyNet-esque robot jobs apocalypse—it’s DOGE firing tens of thousands of federal employees while waving the banner of “an AI-first strategy.”
brian-merchant.work: The AI jobs crisis is here, now
brian-merchant.why: He places the real AI danger in present management uses of AI rather than autonomous machines, and ends his GPT-5 piece urging readers to 'forget the speculative futures'.

curtis-yarvin.q: What they should not fear, though, is the LLM robot revolution.
curtis-yarvin.why: Right after saying everyone should fear the economic impact of LLMs, he says the autonomous-AI takeover is not the thing to fear.

daniel-kokotajlo.q: I predict that under these circumstances the most likely outcome is that we end up with broadly superhuman AGI systems which are in fact misaligned but which the aforementioned small group of decision-makers thinks is aligned.
daniel-kokotajlo.work: Training AGI in Secret would be Unsafe and Unethical
daniel-kokotajlo.why: His central predicted danger is misaligned superhuman AGI, and his Senate testimony likewise centres on superintelligence and automated AI research, not only present-day misuse.

daron-acemoglu.q: my own view is that these concerns are somewhat overblown and often distract from shorter-term problems created by AI technologies (on which this essay has focused), they deserve careful consideration, monitoring and preparation.
daron-acemoglu.why: Discussing the alignment problem, he says superintelligence worries are somewhat overblown and distract from the near-term harms of AI use that his essay focuses on.

david-sacks.q: In my view, the most likely dystopian outcome with AI is a marriage of corporate and state power similar to what we saw exposed in the Twitter Files, where “Trust & Safety” gets weaponized into government censorship and control.
david-sacks.work: Long X post: the 'Goldilocks' state of AI and why the doomer narratives were wrong
david-sacks.why: Having dismissed the superintelligence scenario, he names human use of AI for censorship and control as the main danger.

dean-ball.q: By “catastrophic risks,” I refer to extremely damaging events caused by human misuse or abuse of an advanced AI system. I do not refer to existential risks, or the notion that the AI itself will have a desire to kill or enslave humanity.
dean-ball.work: Before Leviathan Wakes (Why I Believe What I Believe)
dean-ball.why: When describing the one area of AI regulation he supports, he limits it to harms from human misuse and explicitly sets aside autonomous AI turning on humanity.

demis-hassabis.q: But I think that still pales, as a small issue, compared to some of these bigger issues around AGI itself becoming very capable and how do we make sure that guardrails are put in place
demis-hassabis.work: HUGE Conversations with Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis (transcript)
demis-hassabis.why: After discussing deepfakes and misinformation, he calls them small next to the risks from highly capable AGI itself.

dwarkesh-patel.q: People grossly overstate the risks AI poses via misinformation and inequality.
dwarkesh-patel.why: He calls present-day misinformation and inequality harms overstated, and the essay puts the main worry on failing to control models at human level and beyond.

ed-zitron.q: I agree that we need to take “AI safety” seriously, but that starts with treating LLMs as normal software run in a reckless and dangerous manner by malevolent entities with little regard for society.
ed-zitron.work: AI Is Already In Dangerous Hands
ed-zitron.why: Throughout the piece the author argues that safety talk about uncontrollable future AI distracts from the real harms of how labs build and run today's systems, and he closes on this point.

eliezer-yudkowsky.q: The key issue is not “human-competitive” intelligence (as the open letter puts it); it’s what happens after AI gets to smarter-than-human intelligence.
eliezer-yudkowsky.work: The Only Way to Deal With the Threat From AI? Shut It Down
eliezer-yudkowsky.why: He places the central danger in smarter-than-human AI, not in how today's systems are deployed.

emily-m-bender.q: But no, the harms aren’t going to come from autonomous “AI” that just hasn’t been taught appropriate values.
emily-m-bender.work: On NYT Magazine on AI: Resist the Urge to be Impressed
emily-m-bender.why: Her summary says the urgent harms come from how AI is deployed now, not from autonomous AI.

gary-marcus.q: My main AI fears, as I have written before, have mainly been about bad actors, rather than malicious robots per se.
gary-marcus.work: Why my p(doom) has risen, dramatically
gary-marcus.why: He locates his main concern in human misuse of AI rather than autonomous malicious AI.

holly-elmore.q: Other people are attacking X and Meta for chatbot impropriety or OpenAI for being audacious and having a lying CEO. Opposing the attempt to build superintelligence itself is how we fell Anthropic along with all the rest.
holly-elmore.why: She contrasts critiques of present chatbot misbehavior with what she sees as the core issue, the attempt to build superintelligence.

karen-hao.q: not in the X-risk type way, but in terms of now: the impacts that we're seeing on mental health, some leading to devastating consequences, environmental consequences, labor consequences.
karen-hao.why: She places the danger of the AI race in present harms rather than existential risk.

leopold-aschenbrenner.q: At the same time, we will extremely rapidly go from systems where failures are fairly low-stakes (ChatGPT said a bad word, so what)—to extremely high-stakes (oops, the superintelligence self-exfiltrated from our cluster, now it’s hacking the military).
leopold-aschenbrenner.why: He treats present-day failures as low-stakes and places the serious dangers in superintelligent systems.

mark-zuckerberg.q: While it is maybe more intellectually interesting to talk about the existential risks, I actually think the real harms that need more energy in being mitigated are things where someone takes a model and does something to hurt a person.
mark-zuckerberg.work: Mark Zuckerberg: Llama 3, open sourcing $10b models, & Caesar Augustus
mark-zuckerberg.why: Responding on existential risk, he says people misusing models today is where more mitigation energy is needed.

max-tegmark.q: But saying that we therefore shouldn’t talk about the existential threat from superintelligence because it distracts doom these challenges is like saying we shouldn’t talk about a literal inbound asteroid because it distracts from climate change.
max-tegmark.work: The 'Don't Look Up' Thinking That Could Doom Us With AI
max-tegmark.why: After listing present-day harms he supports addressing, he argues superintelligence risk must not be sidelined by them.

meredith-whittaker.q: kind of a, you know, technically grounded concern about the rush to integrate technologies  that are not fit for purpose and could have collateral consequences, which is where I land on it.
meredith-whittaker.work: Meredith Whittaker on Who Controls Your Data in the Age of AI
meredith-whittaker.why: Asked about AI's threat level, she places her concern on rushed deployment of unfit systems and on concentrated corporate power, not on superintelligence.

peter-thiel.q: Maybe it doesn't become a godlike intelligence, which is some of the sort of futuristic transhumanist nonsense. But it could just be this autonomous weapon system on a drone where we want to make them autonomous, because if you have a human in the loop, the human gets jammed.
peter-thiel.work: Apocalypse Now? Peter Thiel on Ancient Prophecies and Modern Tech
peter-thiel.why: He dismisses godlike AI as transhumanist nonsense and locates the danger in how people deploy AI, such as autonomous weapons.

samuel-hammond.q: Lower-tier AI risks, like from the proliferation of deepfakes, are collective action problems that will be primarily mitigated through defensive technologies and institutional adaptation.
samuel-hammond.why: He ranks present misuse such as deepfakes as 'lower-tier' and directs attention to frontier and superintelligence risks.

timnit-gebru.q: Talk of sentient machines only distracts us from holding them accountable for the exploitative labor practices that power the “AI” industry.
timnit-gebru.work: The Exploited Labor Behind Artificial Intelligence
timnit-gebru.why: She argues that attention to sentient or superintelligent machines distracts from present harms in how AI is built and deployed.

venkatesh-rao.q: The clearest live adversarial problem involving AI is much more ordinary: humans using AI against other humans.
venkatesh-rao.work: The Accelerationist Case for Frontier Pacing
venkatesh-rao.why: He contrasts concrete human misuse (crime, weapons diffusion) with fears of vague runaway AGIs, which he finds largely unpersuasive.

vitalik-buterin.q: as well as my caution around a few specific concerns, largely centered around superintelligent AI, and the risk that it may bring about either doom, or irreversible human disempowerment, if the technology is built in the wrong ways.
vitalik-buterin.why: He says his main AI concerns center on superintelligent AI causing doom or human disempowerment, not on present deployment.

william-macaskill.q: The risk of AI takeover is getting increasing attention, but it’s still much more neglected than it should be.
william-macaskill.why: He holds that the risk of takeover by misaligned advanced AI deserves more attention than it gets, not less.

yoshua-bengio.q: But what I’m most worried about today is increasing agency of AI.
yoshua-bengio.work: The Catastrophic Risks of AI — and a Safer Path (transcript)
yoshua-bengio.why: His greatest concern is autonomous, agentic AI, and he argues elsewhere that loss-of-control risks deserve attention alongside present harms.

zvi-mowshowitz.q: Where ‘it’ is superintelligence, and ‘dies’ is that probably everyone on the planet literally dies.
zvi-mowshowitz.work: New Statement Calls For Not Building Superintelligence For Now
zvi-mowshowitz.why: He treats loss of control to superintelligence as the central danger, likely killing everyone.

arvind-narayanan.q: But they should reject the kind of policies that might seem compelling if we view x-risk as urgent and serious, notably: restricting AI development.
arvind-narayanan.work: AI existential risk probabilities are too unreliable to inform policy
arvind-narayanan.why: In their concluding policy advice, the authors tell governments to reject restricting AI development.

bernie-sanders.q: We must place an immediate pause on advanced-AI development and ban artificial superintelligence—an artificial mind smarter than any human, capable of operating independently beyond our control—until a new federal body is able to ensure the technology’s safety.
bernie-sanders.work: Don't Let Big Tech Dictate Humanity's Future
bernie-sanders.why: He explicitly calls for pausing advanced AI development and banning superintelligence.

daniel-kokotajlo.q: If that decreased to, for example, 10%, this would significantly slow down their race towards research automation while freeing up compute to go towards beneficial deployments, safety research, and also simply lowering prices for consumers.
daniel-kokotajlo.why: He recommends deliberately redirecting compute to slow the frontier labs' race toward automating AI research.

dario-amodei.q: a coalition of democracies seeks to gain a clear advantage (even just a temporary one) on powerful AI by securing its supply chain, scaling quickly, and blocking or delaying adversaries’ access to key resources like chips and semiconductor equipment.
dario-amodei.why: His preferred strategy has democracies scale powerful AI quickly rather than deliberately slowing frontier development (only adversaries are delayed).

david-sacks.q: We have 5 major American companies vigorously competing on frontier models. This brings out the best in everyone and helps America win the AI race.
david-sacks.work: Long X post: the 'Goldilocks' state of AI and why the doomer narratives were wrong
david-sacks.why: He celebrates vigorous frontier competition as helping America win, the opposite of deliberately slowing it.

dean-ball.q: I am opposed to pauses and bans on AI development.
dean-ball.work: Before Leviathan Wakes (Why I Believe What I Believe)
dean-ball.why: A direct statement that he opposes slowing or stopping AI development on purpose.

ed-zitron.q: we need to start arresting people for committing crimes, halting any and all training runs, and putting real safeguards on this technology
ed-zitron.work: AI Is Already In Dangerous Hands
ed-zitron.why: The author calls for halting all training runs. His reason is that the labs are irresponsible, not that AI is powerful, and elsewhere he rejects the safety movement's 'slowdown' framing, but the policy he states is a stop.

eliezer-yudkowsky.q: The moratorium on new large training runs needs to be indefinite and worldwide.
eliezer-yudkowsky.work: The Only Way to Deal With the Threat From AI? Shut It Down
eliezer-yudkowsky.why: He calls for an indefinite global halt on large training runs.

guillaume-verdon.q: Because at least to me, I don’t think stagnation or slowing down is actually an option.
guillaume-verdon.work: Guillaume Verdon: Beff Jezos, E/acc Movement, Physics, Computation & AGI (Lex Fridman Podcast #407)
guillaume-verdon.why: He rejects slowing down, and elsewhere opposes slowing AI to a few players.

holly-elmore.q: We need to Pause frontier AI development if we’re ever going to have time and latitude to even see if superintelligence could be safe and respect human consent.
holly-elmore.work: YOU have the power: my Stop the AI Race speech
holly-elmore.why: In her protest speech she directly calls for pausing frontier AI development.

jack-clark.q: We will need to build the infrastructure to take advantage of this technology, but we will also need to go slowly and deliberately on developing the technology itself, to pace or otherwise control its development.
jack-clark.work: Import AI 477: In which I tell the IMF the Singularity has begun
jack-clark.why: The author explicitly calls for pacing AI development, and in another talk says a coordinated global slowdown 'would likely be a good thing'.

jason-crawford.q: But in contrast to defeatist pessimism, we should do this not in order to slow or stop progress, but to identify positive steps we can take towards safer technology.
jason-crawford.work: A plea for solutionism on AI safety
jason-crawford.why: In his summary of 'solutionism' on AI safety, he says identifying risks should not be used to slow or stop AI development.

jd-vance.q: And to restrict its development now would not only unfairly benefit incumbents in the space, it would mean paralyzing one of the most promising technologies we have seen in generations.
jd-vance.work: Remarks by the Vice President at the Artificial Intelligence Action Summit in Paris, France
jd-vance.why: He states the administration's view that restricting AI development now would be a serious mistake.

marc-andreessen.q: We believe any deceleration of AI will cost lives. Deaths that were preventable by the AI that was prevented from existing is a form of murder.
marc-andreessen.why: He opposes any deceleration of AI, likening it to murder.

max-tegmark.q: So let's not pause AI. Let's just pause the reckless race to superintelligence. Let's stop obsessively training ever-larger models that we don't understand.
max-tegmark.work: How to Keep AI Under Control
max-tegmark.why: He calls for pausing the race to superintelligence and stopping the training of ever-larger models, while keeping other AI.

nick-land.q: Any problem whatsoever that we might have would be better answered by a superior mind. Ergo, our instrumental but also absolute priority is the realization of superior minds.
nick-land.why: In his own restatement of the will-to-think, he makes building superior minds the absolute priority, which rejects slowing or stopping it.

noah-smith.q: I believe that this is our best bet for getting China on board for a joint international AI “pacing” effort.
noah-smith.work: Two missing pieces in the AI safety discussion
noah-smith.why: The essay assumes and backs a coordinated slowdown ('pacing') of frontier AI, and proposes how to bring China into it.

paul-kingsnorth.q: You could bomb the data-centres, which — if they were developing superhuman AI — would be a good idea.
paul-kingsnorth.work: Paul Kingsnorth: how to fight the Machine
paul-kingsnorth.why: He endorses destroying superhuman-AI development as a good idea in principle, while doubting it would work unless people change how they see.

peter-thiel.q: At the same time if there is no other vector of growth in our society, we would be out of our minds not to take it.
peter-thiel.work: 'I've been allergic to AI for a long time': an interview with Peter Thiel
peter-thiel.why: Despite reservations about the AI revolution, he says it would be crazy not to pursue AI, which rejects deliberately slowing or stopping it.

robin-hanson.q: Thus when facing the risk of our fear essentially halting progress here, I’d rather continue down our current path, and work harder on controls when we better see concrete serious control problems to manage.
robin-hanson.why: He prefers continuing AI progress over slowing it.

scott-alexander.q: That doesn’t mean I have to support AI accelerationism because 20% is smaller than 50%. Short, carefully-tailored pauses could improve the chance of AI going well by a lot, without increasing the risk of social collapse too much.
scott-alexander.work: Pause For Thought: The AI Pause Debate
scott-alexander.why: In his own concluding comments on the pause debate, he endorses short, tailored pauses of frontier AI while rejecting both accelerationism and indefinite bans.

timnit-gebru.q: We urge researchers in AI to stop their quest to build a system that even those in favor of AGI concede is not well-defined.
timnit-gebru.work: The TESCREAL bundle: Eugenics and the promise of utopia through artificial general intelligence
timnit-gebru.why: She calls on researchers to stop the attempt to build AGI, the most general AI systems.

tyler-cowen.q: We should take the plunge. We already have taken the plunge. We designed/tolerated our decentralized society so we could take the plunge.
tyler-cowen.work: Existential risk, AI, and the inevitable turn in human history
tyler-cowen.why: Answering whether to halt or slow AI, he concludes we should proceed.

venkatesh-rao.q: So yes, pace the frontier. But don’t turn the frontier labs into a cartel to do it.
venkatesh-rao.work: The Accelerationist Case for Frontier Pacing
venkatesh-rao.why: He endorses deliberately managing (pacing) the rate of frontier AI advance, preferably through market signals rather than a cartel.

yann-lecun.q: Or is the strategy to, on the contrary, open it up as widely as possible, so that progress is as fast as possible, so that the bad guys always trail behind? And I'm very much of the second category of thinking.
yann-lecun.work: Meta's AI Chief Yann LeCun on AGI, Open-Source, and AI Risk
yann-lecun.why: On powerful future systems, he favours making progress as fast as possible rather than holding it back.

yoshua-bengio.q: Slowing down AI research and deployment in directions of high risk in order to protect the public, society and humanity from catastrophic outcomes would be worthwhile
yoshua-bengio.why: He explicitly endorses deliberately slowing high-risk AI development.

zvi-mowshowitz.q: We should not build superintelligence until such time as that changes, and the risk of everyone dying as a result, as well as the risk of losing control over the future as a result, is very low.
zvi-mowshowitz.work: New Statement Calls For Not Building Superintelligence For Now
zvi-mowshowitz.why: He supports a prohibition on building superintelligence until its risks are very low, and signed the FLI statement calling for this.

audrey-tang.q: I want the entire world to know that we currently know almost nothing about the actual shape of AI risks, and which is why I signed, in a way, to basically say that this is a global priority alongside the other two, which we know much more about.
audrey-tang.work: 2026-01-20 Doom Debate (Doom Debates, with Liron Shapira)
audrey-tang.why: Explaining why she signed the AI extinction-risk statement alongside pandemic and nuclear war, she treats AI extinction risk as a real global priority while saying its size is unknown (P(Doom) 0-100%).

balaji-srinivasan.q: how how is AI risk real? Just turn it off. The whole thing is set up for you to be able to turn it off.
balaji-srinivasan.work: Why Balaji Srinivasan Thinks the SaaS Apocalypse Is Overhyped (a16z; published by a16z as 'Balaji on Why AI Raises the Cost of Verification')
balaji-srinivasan.why: In a passage arguing against Skynet scenarios, he dismisses AI takeover risk because AI is built with an off switch and cannot reproduce itself.

bernie-sanders.q: AI is an existential threat to humanity. It must be treated as such.
bernie-sanders.work: Don't Let Big Tech Dictate Humanity's Future
bernie-sanders.why: He states directly that AI is an existential threat to humanity.

curtis-yarvin.q: Nonetheless, our argument is that there is zero risk to humanity from arbitrary virtual intelligence.
curtis-yarvin.why: The essay's stated thesis is that AI poses zero risk to humanity, which negates a real extinction risk.

daniel-kokotajlo.q: Maybe causing an existential catastrophe is easier, or quicker, than accelerating world GWP growth. Both seem plausible to me.
daniel-kokotajlo.work: Against GDP as a metric for timelines and takeoff speeds
daniel-kokotajlo.why: He states in his own voice that an AI-related existential catastrophe is plausible.

david-sacks.q: This is the stuff of great engineering and should be celebrated. It’s just not the stuff of apocalyptic pronouncements. Oppenheimer has left the building.
david-sacks.work: Long X post: the 'Goldilocks' state of AI and why the doomer narratives were wrong
david-sacks.why: In a post arguing 'the Doomer narratives were wrong', he says current AI progress gives no basis for apocalyptic claims.

dean-ball.q: It is not any one of these things, but the combination of them, that gives me high confidence that AI existential risk is highly unlikely and thus not worth extreme policy mitigations
dean-ball.work: 2023 (Or, Why I am Not a Doomer)
dean-ball.why: In the section titled 'Why I am Not a Doomer' he concludes with high confidence that existential risk is highly unlikely, and adds that 'If anyone builds it, everyone dies' is false.

demis-hassabis.q: in my view, there's still significant risk, and we've got to do research carefully to quantify what that risk is
demis-hassabis.work: Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis on AGI and AI in the Military
demis-hassabis.why: Asked whether AI power-seeking and escaping human control and disempowering humans is a default path or tail risk, he says the risk is unknown but still significant.

dwarkesh-patel.q: But Marc dismisses the concern that we may fail to control models, especially as they reach human level and beyond. And that’s where I disagree.
dwarkesh-patel.why: In an essay defending people who see AI as an existential risk, the author says he disagrees with dismissing the loss-of-control concern.

ed-zitron.q: never realized that at any time one of the near-cultist types that joined their companies and heard everybody talking in terms of “p(doom)” (fuck off) could take it all seriously and the media might believe them.
ed-zitron.work: AI Is Already In Dangerous Hands
ed-zitron.why: The author dismisses p(doom) talk as something only 'near-cultist types' would take seriously, treating extinction-risk claims as industry scaremongering rather than a real risk.

eliezer-yudkowsky.q: If somebody builds a too-powerful AI, under present conditions, I expect that every single member of the human species and all biological life on Earth dies shortly thereafter.
eliezer-yudkowsky.work: The Only Way to Deal With the Threat From AI? Shut It Down
eliezer-yudkowsky.why: He states directly that he expects human extinction from building too-powerful AI.

elon-musk.q: AI is a fundamental existential risk for human civilization, and I don’t think people fully appreciate that.
elon-musk.work: Elon Musk Governor's Interview (NGA 2017, AI segment transcript)
elon-musk.why: Speaking to the governors, Musk states in his own voice that AI is an existential risk to civilization; later texts repeat a 10-20% chance of annihilation.

emily-m-bender.q: But no, the harms aren’t going to come from autonomous “AI” that just hasn’t been taught appropriate values.
emily-m-bender.work: On NYT Magazine on AI: Resist the Urge to be Impressed
emily-m-bender.why: She dismisses harm from autonomous misaligned AI, the source of extinction scenarios, as a strawman problem.

gary-marcus.q: My p(doom) is still lower than most industry people’s. I am at maybe 3% now, much higher than a month ago
gary-marcus.work: Why my p(doom) has risen, dramatically
gary-marcus.why: After earlier calling literal extinction very unlikely, the author states his updated p(doom) as about 3%, a real if small risk.

geoffrey-hinton.q: There is also a longer term existential threat that will arise when we create digital beings that are more intelligent than ourselves.
geoffrey-hinton.why: He names an existential threat from AI smarter than humans.

helen-toner.q: The classic AI risks—catastrophic misuse, catastrophic misalignment—could indeed be game over for dynamism, so we need to handle those.
helen-toner.work: In search of a dynamist vision for safe superhuman AI
helen-toner.why: Right after agreeing that dynamism is no help 'if all the humans are dead or totally disempowered', she affirms in her own voice that catastrophic misalignment could be game over and must be handled.

holly-elmore.q: A catastrophic accident could easily kill everyone on the plane— human extinction.
holly-elmore.why: Using a plane metaphor for the rush to the Singularity, she says in her own voice that the expected outcome includes human extinction.

jack-clark.q: one can concoct plausible scenarios by which AI could kill every single person on the planet. To think building this technology is without risk would be an act of hubris or insanity.
jack-clark.work: Import AI 458: Reckoning with the future; and a singularity story
jack-clark.why: The author says, in his own voice, that scenarios in which AI kills everyone are plausible.

leopold-aschenbrenner.q: Humanity barely evaded self-destruction during the Cold War. On the historical view, the greatest existential risk posed by AGI is that it will enable us to develop extraordinary new means of mass death.
leopold-aschenbrenner.work: IIId. The Free World Must Prevail
leopold-aschenbrenner.why: He names an existential risk from AGI as real (via new means of mass death), even while elsewhere saying he is not a doomer about misalignment.

marc-andreessen.q: A shorter description of what AI isn’t: Killer software and robots that will spring to life and decide to murder the human race or otherwise ruin everything, like you see in the movies.
marc-andreessen.work: Why AI Will Save the World
marc-andreessen.why: He opens by stating AI will not destroy the world and dismisses the human-extinction scenario as movie fiction.

max-tegmark.q: Sadly, I now feel that we’re living the movie “Don’t look up” for another existential threat: unaligned superintelligence.
max-tegmark.work: The 'Don't Look Up' Thinking That Could Doom Us With AI
max-tegmark.why: Tegmark calls unaligned superintelligence an existential threat in his own voice.

meredith-whittaker.q: AI being on the cusp of, you know,  breaking into full consciousness and perhaps endangering human life. All of this almost like  religious, um, religious rhetoric kind of builds up in response to chat GPT.
meredith-whittaker.work: Signal's President on AI, Advertising, and Running a Popular Messaging App
meredith-whittaker.why: In her own voice she dismisses claims that AI may endanger human life as near-religious rhetoric built around a marketing moment, not a real risk.

nick-land.q: Nothing human makes it out of the near-future.
nick-land.why: He asserts as a forecast that nothing human survives the coming technocapital singularity.

noah-smith.q: But if the biologists are wrong, and the AI of 2027 or 2032 or 2049 can design doomsday viruses, the consequence could be that our whole species dies.
noah-smith.work: Two missing pieces in the AI safety discussion
noah-smith.why: He argues that AI-designed bioweapons are a credible path to human extinction and that the public should worry about it.

paul-kingsnorth.q: If AI doesn’t kill us, it will certainly render us incapable of understanding what reality is.
paul-kingsnorth.why: Speaking in his own voice, he treats AI killing us as a live possibility rather than a negligible one.

peter-thiel.q: And in some sense, the scary answer is there's some truth to all of them.
peter-thiel.work: Apocalypse Now? Peter Thiel on Ancient Prophecies and Modern Tech
peter-thiel.why: Discussing existential risks that include weaponized AI and autonomous weapons, Thiel says there is some truth to all of them, i.e. the risk is real.

sam-altman.q: Development of superhuman machine intelligence (SMI) [1] is probably the greatest threat to the continued existence of humanity.
sam-altman.why: He calls superhuman machine intelligence probably the greatest threat to humanity's continued existence.

samuel-hammond.q: Creating a superintelligence is inherently dangerous and destabilizing, independent of the hardness of alignment.
samuel-hammond.why: In theses treating AI x-risk as real (e.g. 'Dismissing AGI risks as sci-fi is a failure of imagination'), he calls building superintelligence inherently dangerous.

scott-alexander.q: I believe - just like Geoff Hinton, Bill Gates, Sam Altman, Daniel Dennett, etc - that there’s a pretty serious risk of human extinction from AI over the next few decades.
scott-alexander.work: In Continued Defense Of Effective Altruism
scott-alexander.why: The author states in his own voice that he believes there is a serious risk of human extinction from AI.

timnit-gebru.q: But the idea of superintelligent machines with their own agency and decision-making power is not only far from reality — it distracts us from the real risks to human lives surrounding the development and deployment of AI systems.
timnit-gebru.work: The Exploited Labor Behind Artificial Intelligence
timnit-gebru.why: She calls the superintelligent-machine scenario far from reality and contrasts it with the 'real risks'.

venkatesh-rao.q: It is just fun to think about AIs going “sentient” and “super” and “general” and turning evil and stomping on us all to maximize paperclips and so on. But this philosophy of AI is about as serious as literalist religion
venkatesh-rao.why: Closing an essay arguing that fears of a destroying superintelligence are philosophical nonsense, he says the AI-doom view deserves to be taken 'not at all' seriously.

vitalik-buterin.q: One way in which AI gone wrong could make the world worse is (almost) the worst possible way: it could literally cause human extinction.
vitalik-buterin.why: He states in his own voice that AI could cause extinction and later says the arguments make it 'worth worrying at least a little bit'.

william-macaskill.q: Explosive technological progress could lead to new weapons and other destructive technologies. This could increase the risk of global catastrophe, including human extinction
william-macaskill.why: In listing grand challenges of an AI-driven intelligence explosion, he treats human extinction as a real risk, alongside a 'substantial' risk of AI takeover.

yann-lecun.q: It's not like one day, we’re going to build some gigantic computer and turn it on, and then the next minute it is going to take over the world. That's the preposterous scenario.
yann-lecun.work: Meta's AI Chief Yann LeCun on AGI, Open-Source, and AI Risk
yann-lecun.why: Answering why he calls AI existential risk preposterous, he dismisses the takeover scenario outright.

yoshua-bengio.q: given the magnitude of the potentially negative impact (up to human extinction), it is imperative to invest more in both understanding and quantifying the risks and developing mitigating solutions.
yoshua-bengio.work: Reasoning through arguments against taking AI safety seriously
yoshua-bengio.why: He treats human extinction from AI as a real possibility that demands investment in mitigation.

zvi-mowshowitz.q: Building superintelligence poses large existential risks. Also known as: If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies.
zvi-mowshowitz.work: New Statement Calls For Not Building Superintelligence For Now
zvi-mowshowitz.why: He states in his own voice that superintelligence poses large existential risks.

audrey-tang.q: But in other places, where people simply say, “Oh, it’s just a machine, it cannot do superhuman persuasion, and stochastic parrot, and so on,” then I would say it’s probably below the optimal level.
audrey-tang.work: 2026-01-20 Doom Debate (Doom Debates, with Liron Shapira)
audrey-tang.why: Asked whether public fear of AI is at the right level, she says Taiwan's is about optimal and elsewhere it is below what is warranted, not above.

balaji-srinivasan.q: Then people are just scared of the thing that they themselves created, right?
balaji-srinivasan.work: Why Balaji Srinivasan Thinks the SaaS Apocalypse Is Overhyped (a16z; published by a16z as 'Balaji on Why AI Raises the Cost of Verification')
balaji-srinivasan.why: He describes fears of a Terminator-style AI as people frightening themselves with their own prompts, not as a response to real evidence.

bernie-sanders.q: The American people see what is coming. And they don’t like it.
bernie-sanders.work: Artificial intelligence is coming for the working class. We must fight back
bernie-sanders.why: Citing polls of public concern about AI job losses, he endorses those fears as an accurate reading of what is coming.

dario-amodei.q: I think that most people are underestimating just how radical the upside of AI could be, just as I think most people are underestimating how bad the risks could be.
dario-amodei.why: He says most people underestimate AI's risks, the opposite of fear exceeding the evidence (though he also criticises some 2023-24 voices as sensationalist).

david-sacks.q: This means that apocalyptic predictions of job loss are as overhyped as AGI itself.
david-sacks.work: Long X post: the 'Goldilocks' state of AI and why the doomer narratives were wrong
david-sacks.why: He calls fears of AI job loss and of AGI overhyped relative to what models can actually do.

demis-hassabis.q: I think the public’s right to be concerned.
demis-hassabis.work: Demis Hassabis Thinks We're in the 'Foothills of the Singularity'
demis-hassabis.why: Asked about negative public perception of AI, he says the concern is justified and that he shares several of the worries.

ed-zitron.q: Everybody doing backflips out of fear about “powerful, autonomous AI breaking out of the sandbox” is mostly doing so because a British guy went on TV and said “AI will kill us all,”
ed-zitron.work: AI Is Already In Dangerous Hands
ed-zitron.why: The author says public fear of autonomous AI rests on media hype, not on what the technology does, a point he repeats about the 'white collar bloodbath' stories.

eliezer-yudkowsky.q: A large amount of failure to panic sufficiently, seems to me to stem from a lack of appreciation for the incredible potential lethality of this thing that Earthlings as a culture have not named.
eliezer-yudkowsky.work: AGI Ruin: A List of Lethalities
eliezer-yudkowsky.why: He says people are not afraid enough, the opposite of fear exceeding the evidence.

elon-musk.q: I have exposure to the most cutting edge AI, and I think people should be really concerned about it. I keep sounding the alarm bell.
elon-musk.work: Elon Musk Governor's Interview (NGA 2017, AI segment transcript)
elon-musk.why: He says the public is under-concerned about AI rather than over-concerned, the opposite of the statement.

geoffrey-hinton.q: And that got me very worried and it should get you very worried too.
geoffrey-hinton.work: Will AI outsmart human intelligence? (Royal Institution lecture, transcript)
geoffrey-hinton.why: He tells his audience they should be more worried about digital intelligence, not less.

jack-clark.q: But mostly, I think we need to listen: Generally, people know what’s going on. We must do a better job of listening to the concerns people have.
jack-clark.work: Import AI 431: Technological Optimism and Appropriate Fear
jack-clark.why: In a talk titled 'Appropriate Fear', where he says he is deeply afraid himself, he treats public concerns about AI as well founded.

jd-vance.q: And I think there's too much fear that AI will simply replace jobs rather than augmenting so many of the things that we do.
jd-vance.work: Remarks by the Vice President at the American Dynamism Summit
jd-vance.why: He says public fear about AI replacing jobs is excessive.

marc-andreessen.q: In contrast to this positive view, the public conversation about AI is presently shot through with hysterical fear and paranoia.
marc-andreessen.work: Why AI Will Save the World
marc-andreessen.why: He characterises current public fear of AI as hysterical and paranoid, i.e. beyond what is warranted.

max-tegmark.q: Think again: instead, the most influential responses have been a combination of denial, mockery, and resignation so darkly comical that it’s deserving of an Oscar.
max-tegmark.work: The 'Don't Look Up' Thinking That Could Doom Us With AI
max-tegmark.why: He says the public response to AI risk has been denial and mockery, the opposite of excessive fear.

paul-kingsnorth.q: Calm down, they all say, stop all the Matrix talk. There are dangers, yes, but this is just hysteria. Notably, though, as we saw last time, the people actually running the show do not talk like this.
paul-kingsnorth.why: He presents the 'it's just hysteria' view in order to dismiss it, citing the developers' own fears as evidence that the alarm is warranted.

robin-hanson.q: Many of these fears, however, are either unfounded or overblown.
robin-hanson.why: He says most AI fears are unfounded or overblown, driven by ignorance and fear of change.

sam-altman.q: The fear and anxiety about AI is justified; we are in the process of witnessing the largest change to society in a long time, and perhaps ever.
sam-altman.work: Untitled post, shown on the blog as "-"
sam-altman.why: He explicitly says public fear and anxiety about AI are justified.

venkatesh-rao.q: I sincerely believe their fears are strictly nonsensical in a philosophical sense, in the same sense that I consider fear of ghosts or going to hell in an “afterlife” to be strictly nonsensical.
venkatesh-rao.why: He states in his own voice that the special fears of AI common in popular discourse are unfounded, comparable to fear of ghosts.

yann-lecun.q: People have been saying, “Oh my God, we need to regulate LLMs because they’re gonna be so dangerous.” That is just not true.
yann-lecun.work: Meta's AI Chief Yann LeCun on AGI, Open-Source, and AI Risk
yann-lecun.why: Citing a RAND study showing no bioweapon uplift, he says the claimed dangers of current systems are untrue.

zvi-mowshowitz.q: As we find out more about that, a lot of people have grown far more alarmed, as they should given what they previously believed about the difficulty of alignment
zvi-mowshowitz.why: He says growing public alarm is warranted by the evidence, not excessive.

audrey-tang.q: Because when an exit is real, then the platform must compete on care, not on capture.
audrey-tang.work: 2025-11-10 Berlin Freedom Conference: The Role of AI
audrey-tang.why: Arguing for portability and interoperability, she says real competition (exit) disciplines platforms into caring for users rather than capturing them.

david-sacks.q: At least when you have multiple strong private sector players, that gets harder. By contrast, winner-take-all dynamics are more likely to produce Orwellian outcomes.
david-sacks.work: Long X post: the 'Goldilocks' state of AI and why the doomer narratives were wrong
david-sacks.why: He argues competition among several AI firms makes abusive control harder.

guillaume-verdon.q: And ultimately the thesis is that the market will positively select for AIs that are more reliable, more safe and tend to be aligned, they do what you want them to do, right.
guillaume-verdon.work: Guillaume Verdon: Beff Jezos, E/acc Movement, Physics, Computation & AGI (Lex Fridman Podcast #407)
guillaume-verdon.why: He holds that market competition, with liability, pushes AI toward safety.

marc-andreessen.q: When market discipline is absent, there is no limit to how crazy things can get. The motto of every monopoly and cartel, every centralized institution not subject to market discipline: “We don’t care, because we don’t have to.” Markets prevent monopolies and cartels.
marc-andreessen.why: He argues that market discipline is what checks bad behaviour by sellers and prevents monopolies and cartels.

robin-hanson.q: Today such rents are non-trivial, but even so competition between orgs keeps them tolerable.
robin-hanson.why: He holds that competition keeps harms from organizations tolerable and expects the same for AIs.

scott-alexander.q: so companies in an economic environment of sufficiently intense competition are forced to abandon all values except optimizing-for-profit or else be outcompeted by companies that optimized for profit better
scott-alexander.why: His central argument is that intense market competition drives firms to sacrifice values such as worker welfare, the opposite of competition limiting harm.

yoshua-bengio.q: The competitive nature of capitalism is clearly also a cause for concern as a potential source of careless AI design motivated by profits and winning market share that could lead to potentially rogue AIs.
yoshua-bengio.why: He sees market competition as a source of dangerous AI design rather than a check on harm.

audrey-tang.q: And plurality is saying, “Okay, this singularity view, where people collectively lose control of the hamster wheel, is the bad ending, and we want the good ending, where the AI systems are like campfires, bonfires that people gather around
audrey-tang.work: 2026-01-20 Doom Debate (Doom Debates, with Liron Shapira)
audrey-tang.why: Defining Plurality, she calls the singularity the bad ending and wants AI that helps communities connect and bridge their differences.

e-glen-weyl.q: I increasingly use the terms “pluralist” to describe myself and “Plurality” to describe the direction I want to see technology go in.
e-glen-weyl.why: He names Plurality, defined in the essay as fostering cooperation across diverse groups, as the direction he wants technology to take, in contrast to the totalism of dominant AI visions.

guillaume-verdon.q: Effective Accelerationism, e/acc, is a set of ideas and practices that seek tomaximize the probability of the technocapital singularity, and subsequently, the ability for emergent consciousness to flourish.
guillaume-verdon.why: The manifesto sets maximizing the probability of a technocapital singularity as the movement's goal.

holly-elmore.q: The work of civilization is not obtaining more powerful technology, but determining how to govern the gains of technology fairly and in a way that respects the many different needs and values of the Galaxy.
holly-elmore.why: Describing the 'Star Trek future' she says she and her colleague prefer over Singularity futures, she puts the governance of diverse needs ahead of more powerful technology.

pope-leo-xiv.q: It means freeing technology from monopolistic control and opening it to discussion and debate, therefore making it human-friendly and restoring it to the plurality of human cultures and ways of life.
pope-leo-xiv.work: Magnifica Humanitas: Encyclical on safeguarding the human person in the time of Artificial Intelligence
pope-leo-xiv.why: He wants technology returned to the plurality of human cultures, and elsewhere rejects a 'technological divinization' as the path to fulfilment.

balaji-srinivasan.q: The billions of people who just got their first smartphone have had their lives dramatically improved as a consequence, and are too pragmatic to romanticize the past.
balaji-srinivasan.why: In an essay urging people to champion technological progress, he says consumer technology has greatly improved billions of lives.

david-sacks.q: the current state of vigorous competition is healthy. It propels innovation forward, helps America win the AI race, and avoids centralized control.
david-sacks.work: Long X post: the 'Goldilocks' state of AI and why the doomer narratives were wrong
david-sacks.why: He calls market competition in AI healthy and good news, praising its results.

dean-ball.q: I approach all matters of AI policy with an intrinsically techno-optimist sensibility. This means that I believe the net effect of technology on human beings has been not just modestly but overwhelmingly good, on average, throughout our history.
dean-ball.work: 2023 (Or, Why I am Not a Doomer)
dean-ball.why: He states as his own view that technology has been overwhelmingly good for people, and he pairs this elsewhere with a classical-liberal preference for markets over regulation.

dwarkesh-patel.q: Technological progress throughout history has dramatically improved our quality of life.
dwarkesh-patel.why: In his list of points where he agrees with Andreessen, he affirms that technological progress has greatly improved life.

guillaume-verdon.q: e.g. a new technological paradigm emerges, letting the free market find how to extract utility from this said technology would be the best way to proceed, much better than fear-mongering
guillaume-verdon.work: Notes on e/acc principles and tenets
guillaume-verdon.why: He holds that the free market is the best way to get value from new technology.

jd-vance.q: Real innovation makes us more productive, but it also, I think, dignifies our workers. It boosts our standard of living.
jd-vance.work: Remarks by the Vice President at the American Dynamism Summit
jd-vance.why: Speaking to tech builders, he says innovation from American companies raises living standards and benefits workers.

leopold-aschenbrenner.q: I am a big believer in the American private sector, and would almost never advocate for heavy government involvement in technology or industry.
leopold-aschenbrenner.why: He states a general belief in private-sector technological development, making superintelligence a stated exception.

marc-andreessen.q: We believe the techno-capital machine is not anti-human – in fact, it may be the most pro-human thing there is. It serves us.
marc-andreessen.why: He calls the combination of markets and technology possibly the most pro-human thing there is.

meredith-whittaker.q: A tool that benefits a small number of people, but often at the expense of the majority.
meredith-whittaker.work: Tech, AI, digital infrastructure and surveillance with Meredith Whittaker
meredith-whittaker.why: She says AI, as built by a few profit-driven companies, benefits a small number of people at the expense of the majority, and she criticises the surveillance business model in general.

mustafa-suleyman.q: We should celebrate and accelerate technology because it’s been the greatest engine of human progress in history.
mustafa-suleyman.why: He states as his own view that technology, built through 'scientific discovery and entrepreneurial application', has been the main driver of human progress.

noah-smith.q: In general, when we look at the past, we understand that technology has almost always made things better for humanity, especially over the long haul.
noah-smith.work: I love AI. Why doesn't everyone?
noah-smith.why: He states as his own view that technology has almost always improved human life over time.

paul-kingsnorth.q: I am seeing ecological destruction, political division, cultural fragmentation and a dark desire to rebuild nature in our own image.
paul-kingsnorth.work: Paul Kingsnorth: 'AI is not just another technology'
paul-kingsnorth.why: Asked whether the fruits of the AI and transhumanist revolution, which he ties to a profit-seeking capitalist Machine, are good, he answers that he sees only harms.

peter-thiel.q: Technology means doing more with less. In the absence of technological progress, we end up with a zero-sum world, in which there must be a loser for every winner.
peter-thiel.why: In an essay defending technological acceleration within a capitalist, growth-dependent economy, he argues technological progress is what keeps life from becoming zero-sum.

sam-altman.q: Capitalism is a powerful engine of economic growth because it rewards people for investing in assets that generate value over time, which is an effective incentive system for creating and distributing technological gains.
sam-altman.why: He endorses capitalism as an effective system for creating and spreading technological gains, while adding that it needs fixes for inequality.

samuel-hammond.q: The accelerationists have the long view of history on their side, and I broadly support the Andreesen vision of the future.
samuel-hammond.why: He broadly endorses the accelerationist view of market-driven technology improving human life, while warning about trade-offs during the transition.

tyler-cowen.q: In my view the good will considerably outweigh the bad (at least from losing #2, not #1), but I do understand that the absolute quantity of the bad disruptions will be high.
tyler-cowen.work: Existential risk, AI, and the inevitable turn in human history
tyler-cowen.why: He judges radical technological change, which 'our decentralized society' was built to absorb, to be net good, as with the printing press and fire.

venkatesh-rao.q: The result was not a world full of useless mouths. It was a world in which vastly more people could do things other than farm, while enjoying access to vastly more food.
venkatesh-rao.why: He presents the market-driven productivity gains of capitalism as broadly liberating and expects AI to follow a similar beneficial pattern.

vitalik-buterin.q: First, on balance technology and economic growth have been massively good for humanity, and any delay to it imposes costs that are hard to overstate.
vitalik-buterin.why: He states as his own view that technology and economic growth have been good for people on balance.

bernie-sanders.q: If AI and robotics become smarter than humans, there is a real possibility they will function independently of human control, with possible catastrophic outcomes. That obviously must not be allowed to happen.
bernie-sanders.work: Artificial intelligence is coming for the working class. We must fight back
bernie-sanders.why: He wants action now to prevent future smarter-than-human systems from escaping human control, before they exist.

daniel-kokotajlo.q: I’ve previously argued that for AI timelines, what we care about is the “point of no return,” the day we lose most of our ability to reduce AI risk.
daniel-kokotajlo.work: Against GDP as a metric for timelines and takeoff speeds
daniel-kokotajlo.why: He argues that our ability to reduce AI risk may be lost well before advanced AI is deployed, so the work has to be done before then.

dario-amodei.q: But in this current essay, I want to confront the rite of passage itself: to map out the risks that we are about to face and try to begin making a battle plan to defeat them.
dario-amodei.why: He sets out to plan defences against the risks of powerful AI before it arrives, which he expects within a few years.

daron-acemoglu.q: they deserve careful consideration, monitoring and preparation.
daron-acemoglu.why: Of alignment concerns about future super-human machines, he says that although somewhat overblown they deserve preparation now; this is a mild hold.

demis-hassabis.q: and then deal with it ahead of time with as much foresight as possible, rather than after the fact, which, with technologies this powerful and this transformative, could be extremely risky.
demis-hassabis.work: Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis on AGI and AI in the Military
demis-hassabis.why: On loss-of-control risk, he says it must be researched and handled before the fact rather than after.

dwarkesh-patel.q: Which means that work to prepare for misaligned 2028 ASI still makes a lot of sense - I think this is a totally plausible outcome.
dwarkesh-patel.work: Why I don't think AGI is right around the corner
dwarkesh-patel.why: Even while arguing for longer timelines, he says preparing now for misaligned superintelligence makes sense.

eliezer-yudkowsky.q: It shows an overwhelming gap between how seriously we are taking the problem, and how seriously we needed to take the problem starting 30 years ago.
eliezer-yudkowsky.work: The Only Way to Deal With the Threat From AI? Shut It Down
eliezer-yudkowsky.why: He argues the safety problem should have been worked on decades before superhuman AI, since failure on the first try is fatal.

elon-musk.q: AI is a rare case where I think we need to be proactive in regulation, instead of reactive.
elon-musk.work: Elon Musk Governor's Interview (NGA 2017, AI segment transcript)
elon-musk.why: He argues that controls on AI must be put in place before harms appear, because reactive regulation would come too late.

gary-marcus.q: We certainly aren’t prepared now, and if we don’t get moving, we won’t be prepared in 10, either.
gary-marcus.work: The 'AI 2027' Scenario: How realistic is it?
gary-marcus.why: Although he doubts AGI in three years, he says preparation for superhuman AI must start now.

geoffrey-hinton.q: We urgently need research on how to prevent these new beings from wanting to take control.
geoffrey-hinton.why: He calls for urgent research on keeping control before AI becomes more intelligent than humans.

helen-toner.q: Advancing the science of aligning/steering/controlling AI systems, especially systems that are advanced enough to realize when they’re being tested.
helen-toner.work: "Long" timelines to advanced AI have gotten crazy short
helen-toner.why: This is on her list of things we 'need to leap into action on' now, because they 'will likely take years and years to bear fruit' before human-level AI arrives.

holly-elmore.q: PauseAI’s most basic stance is that the default should be to pause frontier AI capabilities development to keep us from wading any further into a minefield, to give time for technical safety work to be done, and for proper governance to be established.
holly-elmore.work: The myth of AI 'warning shots' as cavalry
holly-elmore.why: She endorses PauseAI's stance (her own organization's) that safety work and governance must be done before more capable systems are built.

jack-clark.q: We have to get alignment right: Alignment techniques that work today may break under recursive self-improvement as the AI systems become much smarter than the people or systems that supervise them.
jack-clark.work: Import AI 455: AI systems are about to start building themselves.
jack-clark.why: Writing before automated AI R&D exists, which he forecasts for around 2028, the author lists getting alignment right for those future systems as a top implication to work on now.

jason-crawford.q: I see the trend towards greater safety, including safety work before new technologies are introduced, as something fundamentally good.
jason-crawford.work: A plea for solutionism on AI safety
jason-crawford.why: He endorses doing safety work before a technology is introduced, and applies this to AI, urging people to identify AI risks ahead of time.

leopold-aschenbrenner.q: More generally, the more we can develop good science now, the more we’ll be in a position to verify that things aren’t going off the rails during the intelligence explosion.
leopold-aschenbrenner.why: He calls for alignment science to be developed now, ahead of superhuman systems.

max-tegmark.q: I’m part of a a growing AI safety research community that’s working hard to figure out how to make superintelligence aligned, even before it exists, so that it’s goals will be are aligned with human flourishing, or we can somehow control it.
max-tegmark.work: The 'Don't Look Up' Thinking That Could Doom Us With AI
max-tegmark.why: He describes his own work as solving alignment or control of superintelligence before it exists.

mustafa-suleyman.q: I think it's still a good five to 10 years before we have to really confront that. But it's time to start talking about it now.
mustafa-suleyman.why: On recursive self-improvement, he says the danger is years away but the work should start now.

robin-hanson.q: Furthermore, I don’t see why its worth putting much effort into planning how to control AIs far in advance of seeing much detail about how AIs actually do concrete tasks where loss of control matters.
robin-hanson.work: Why Not Wait On AI Risk?
robin-hanson.why: He argues control efforts should wait until concrete systems exist.

sam-altman.q: But we will face this threat at some point, and we have a lot of work to do before it gets here.
sam-altman.why: He argues that safeguards and safety research for SMI should start now, though SMI is probably decades away.

scott-alexander.q: If it turns out that superintelligence is centuries away and such research is premature, little will have been lost. But if our projections were too optimistic, and superintelligence is imminent, then doing such research now rather than later becomes vital.
scott-alexander.why: In his FAQ's closing section on what to do, the author argues that alignment research should be done now, before superintelligence arrives.

william-macaskill.q: AGI preparedness is therefore not just about ensuring that advanced AI systems are aligned: we should be preparing, now, for the disorienting range of developments an intelligence explosion would bring.
william-macaskill.why: He argues that alignment and wider preparation must happen now, before superintelligence arrives, because some challenges come before AI can help solve them.

yoshua-bengio.q: However, sufficient investment in safety is necessary to ensure the safety answers are figured out before reaching AGI, whatever its timeline, and it is not currently what is happening.
yoshua-bengio.work: Reasoning through arguments against taking AI safety seriously
yoshua-bengio.why: He says safety solutions must be found before AGI arrives and that current investment falls short.

zvi-mowshowitz.q: I think it was always valuable to get to thinking about such problems early, as much of this has long lead times and cannot be done in parallel
zvi-mowshowitz.why: He argues that alignment work should start early because of its long lead times.

curtis-yarvin.q: Unlike human abolitionism, “AI abolitionism” cannot happen, because it does not even make sense—it is impossible to construct a sane jurisprudence which includes first-class virtual agents
curtis-yarvin.why: He holds that granting AI any first-class legal or moral standing is incoherent, calling AI a natural and eternal slave.

dwarkesh-patel.q: Giving AIs a stake in the future also means respecting their autonomy and wellbeing.
dwarkesh-patel.work: Give AIs a stake in the future
dwarkesh-patel.why: He says AIs' autonomy and wellbeing should be respected, which grants them moral consideration.

eliezer-yudkowsky.q: we may at some point inadvertently create digital minds which are truly conscious and ought to have rights and shouldn’t be owned.
eliezer-yudkowsky.work: The Only Way to Deal With the Threat From AI? Shut It Down
eliezer-yudkowsky.why: He says, as a moral duty, that AI systems may come to be conscious and merit rights.

guillaume-verdon.q: And ultimately, at some point, these synthetic intelligences are going to make good points about how to steer systems in our civilization, and we should hear them out. And so why should we restrict free speech to biological intelligences only?
guillaume-verdon.work: Guillaume Verdon: Beff Jezos, E/acc Movement, Physics, Computation & AGI (Lex Fridman Podcast #407)
guillaume-verdon.why: He argues free speech should extend to synthetic intelligences.

mustafa-suleyman.q: AIs cannot be people – or moral beings.
mustafa-suleyman.work: We must build AI for people; not to be a person
mustafa-suleyman.why: In an essay warning against 'model welfare', he asserts AIs cannot be moral beings and calls extending moral consideration to them premature and dangerous.

robin-hanson.q: The main danger here is precisely that we might refuse to grant AIs their freedom out of fear.
robin-hanson.why: He argues against enslaving AIs and for granting them freedom.

venkatesh-rao.q: There is another model available: treat sufficiently capable AIs and humans increasingly as peers engaged in negotiated relationships.
venkatesh-rao.why: He criticises Microsoft for rejecting AI personhood and welfare claims and proposes treating capable AIs as peers with legal agency and moral fellowship.

william-macaskill.q: But as soon as you think maybe, and quite probably, those beings have moral status, that no longer looks like an attractive vision for future society.
william-macaskill.work: Will MacAskill on AI causing a 'century in a decade' and how we're completely unprepared
william-macaskill.why: Speaking in his own voice, he says future AI beings quite probably have moral status, which makes a future of pure AI servants unattractive.

daniel-kokotajlo.q: I now think that to a significant extent this race is happening anyway. If we want a serious slowdown, we need to coordinate internationally to all proceed cautiously together.
daniel-kokotajlo.work: Training AGI in Secret would be Unsafe and Unethical
daniel-kokotajlo.why: He says he no longer believes the 'good guys' should race to AGI first, and calls for international coordination to slow down instead.

dario-amodei.q: Export controls serve a vital purpose: keeping democratic nations at the forefront of AI development.
dario-amodei.why: He argues that US and allied AI must stay ahead of China and supports export controls to that end.

david-sacks.q: We must win the AI race, but it matters how we win. Our victory over China will be a Pyrrhic one if we allow our own models to enforce ideological bias, censorship, and historical revisionism akin to CCP AI.
david-sacks.work: Thread on the White House AI Action Plan and Trump's first major AI speech
david-sacks.why: In his own words he frames AI as a race against China that America must win.

dean-ball.q: America is not even remotely on track to do this right now, China is miles ahead of us, and no one, including me, is doing enough to solve this problem.
dean-ball.why: He presents the AI race as a contest America must win by building up manufacturing, and treats China's lead as a problem America urgently needs to solve.

e-glen-weyl.q: If pluralistic societies want to win a race not against China as a nation but against authoritarianism wherever it arises, they cannot make it a race for the development of AI which gives up the game before it begins.
e-glen-weyl.work: AI Is an Ideology, Not a Technology
e-glen-weyl.why: The authors reject framing the contest as a race against China to develop AI, arguing that this framing concedes the game.

eliezer-yudkowsky.q: If the policy starts with the U.S., then China needs to see that the U.S. is not seeking an advantage but rather trying to prevent a horrifically dangerous technology which can have no true owner and which will kill everyone in the U.S. and in China and on Earth.
eliezer-yudkowsky.work: The Only Way to Deal With the Threat From AI? Shut It Down
eliezer-yudkowsky.why: He rejects seeking a US advantage over China in AI, since the technology would kill everyone regardless of who builds it.

gary-marcus.q: I never bought this argument because I figured that getting to GPT-5 first might buy the winner better boilerplate text writing, but not military genius.
gary-marcus.work: The race for "AI Supremacy" is over, at least for now
gary-marcus.why: Discussing export controls meant to secure a US lead over China, he rejects the argument that racing to be first matters.

helen-toner.q: Because of this, I agree that it is a very good thing for the US to have more AI compute, including more AI supercomputers, than China.
helen-toner.work: Building supercomputers for autocrats probably isn't good for democracy, actually
helen-toner.why: Although she criticizes the UAE deal, she says plainly that compute drives national power and that a US lead over China in AI compute is a very good thing.

jd-vance.q: that will pass up on the opportunity to use AI, or any other technology, to advance their own interests and further undermine the interests of their rivals? I think the answer is obvious, and that's why, America, we've got to be tech-forward.
jd-vance.work: Remarks by the Vice President at the American Dynamism Summit
jd-vance.why: He cites China's ambitions as the reason America must push ahead on AI and technology.

karen-hao.q: this what about China card that Silicon Valley has just been able to pull out so effectively again and again and again, if you look at the track record of what this argument has gotten us, it has just gotten us more authoritarianism in the world.
karen-hao.work: Decolonizing the Future: Karen Hao on Resisting the Empire of AI
karen-hao.why: She rejects the China-rivalry argument for clearing the way for tech companies, saying it has produced more authoritarianism.

leopold-aschenbrenner.q: And those who herald the age of AGI in SF too often ignore the elephant in the room: superintelligence is a matter of national security, and the United States must win.
leopold-aschenbrenner.work: IIId. The Free World Must Prevail
leopold-aschenbrenner.why: He frames the AGI race with China as a reason for the US to press ahead and keep its lead.

marc-andreessen.q: And, a whole-of-government program to drive the success of US technology companies globally, against a hostile China and a regulation-crazed EU.
marc-andreessen.why: Among his policy proposals for American technology supremacy he calls for a whole-of-government push framed against a hostile China.

mark-zuckerberg.q: Plus, constraining American innovation to closed development increases the chance that we don’t lead at all.
mark-zuckerberg.work: Open Source AI Is the Path Forward
mark-zuckerberg.why: In the section on how the US should handle states like China, he argues for policy that keeps the US leading and later for a sustainable first-mover advantage.

max-tegmark.q: As if the race to superintelligence were an arms race that would be won by “us” or “them”, when it’s probably a suicide race whose only winner is “it.”
max-tegmark.work: The 'Don't Look Up' Thinking That Could Doom Us With AI
max-tegmark.why: Answering the 'But China!' objection to a pause, he calls the race a suicide race rather than one the US should win.

meredith-whittaker.q: the idea that if the US puts any guardrails, any regulations, any restrictions on the unfettered surveillance and development of AI and other systems it will lose to China is doing a lot of work to, I believe, promote unsafe technologies
meredith-whittaker.work: Tech, AI, digital infrastructure and surveillance with Meredith Whittaker
meredith-whittaker.why: She says the argument from rivalry with China is used to promote unsafe technologies and to brush aside democratic questions.

noah-smith.q: So it’s in America’s interest to preserve its technological edge in AI for as long as possible.
noah-smith.work: America's chip export controls are working
noah-smith.why: He argues that keeping the US lead in AI over China is needed to deter a war, which makes the rivalry his reason for keeping the lead.

pope-leo-xiv.q: This entails a race for ever more powerful algorithms and larger datasets, driven by the desire to secure geopolitical or commercial dominance.
pope-leo-xiv.work: Magnifica Humanitas: Encyclical on safeguarding the human person in the time of Artificial Intelligence
pope-leo-xiv.why: In calling to 'disarm' AI from armed competition, he rejects racing for ever more powerful AI to secure geopolitical dominance, which covers a US-China race.

scott-alexander.q: But then why are you so sure that it’s crucial to “win” the AI “race”? If you’re sure these kinds of thing won’t happen, then you should treat AI like electricity, automobiles, or stealth bombers.
scott-alexander.why: In an essay written against delaying-AI-because-of-China arguments, he argues that outside fast-takeoff scenarios the race to beat China does not matter much, and inside them alignment matters more.

tyler-cowen.q: Importantly, AI offers the potential promise of extending American hegemony just a bit more, a factor of critical importance, as Americans are right now the AI leaders. And should we wait, and get a “more Chinese” version of the alignment problem?
tyler-cowen.work: Existential risk, AI, and the inevitable turn in human history
tyler-cowen.why: He cites American AI leadership over China as a reason not to wait.

dario-amodei.q: A 21st century, AI-enabled polity could be both a stronger protector of individual freedom, and a beacon of hope that helps make liberal democracy the form of government that the whole world wants to adopt.
dario-amodei.why: He treats liberal democracy as the protector of individual freedom, presupposing the two are compatible.

divya-siddarth.q: Unless we carve out room for human self-determination and freedom—the very things we aim to defend in a democracy—we may find ourselves following the gradient toward greater automation without greater autonomy.
divya-siddarth.why: In her own concluding argument she treats freedom as what democracy exists to defend.

jd-vance.q: Now, the good news is that I happen to think your democracies are substantially less brittle than many people apparently fear, and I really do believe that allowing our citizens to speak their mind will make them stronger still.
jd-vance.work: Remarks at the Munich Security Conference
jd-vance.why: He argues that free speech strengthens democracy rather than threatening it.

josh-hawley.q: What we’ve got to do now is recommit ourselves to the fundamental premise that the individual matters, that his liberty matters, and that his ability to participate in, her ability to participate in, democratic life is right at the core of who we are as a country.
josh-hawley.work: Josh Hawley: We Must ‘Bend’ AI to Serve the Good
josh-hawley.why: He treats individual liberty and democratic participation as joint parts of the same national core.

leopold-aschenbrenner.q: I believe in freedom and democracy, strongly, because I don’t know what the right values are.
leopold-aschenbrenner.work: IIId. The Free World Must Prevail
leopold-aschenbrenner.why: He endorses freedom and democracy together as a joint commitment, treating them as compatible.

peter-thiel.q: Most importantly, I no longer believe that freedom and democracy are compatible.
peter-thiel.why: Thiel states in his own voice that he no longer thinks freedom and democracy are compatible.

vitalik-buterin.q: Just like me, he has always found ideas of freedom and ideas of democracy both compelling, and has tried to find the ideal combination of both, that treats them not as opposite goals to be balanced, but as opposite sides of the same coin that need to be integrated.
vitalik-buterin.work: Plurality philosophy in an incredibly oversized nutshell
vitalik-buterin.why: He says that he, like Weyl, sees freedom and democracy as two sides of the same coin to be integrated.

eliezer-yudkowsky.q: But I predict that many of this book’s readers have high-level beliefs similar to those I outlined in Chapter 2, while employing a reasoning style that is really a special case of modest epistemology; and I think that this reasoning style is causing them substantial harm.
eliezer-yudkowsky.why: He argues that modest epistemology, deferring rather than reasoning for oneself, is harmful.

tyler-cowen.q: I hear various views, often from people working in the area, and on the tech per se I have an optimism that corresponds to the weighted average of what I hear.
tyler-cowen.work: Why I think AI take-off is relatively slow
tyler-cowen.why: He explicitly sets his view to the weighted average of informed opinion, and elsewhere says he always sides with the experts.

william-macaskill.q: So, if a chain of reasoning leads us to the conclusion that we’re living in the most important century ever, we should think it more likely that our reasoning has gone wrong than that the conclusion really is true.
william-macaskill.work: Are we living at the most influential time in history?
william-macaskill.why: He argues that a very low base rate should outweigh informal inside-view arguments, defending an 'outside-view' default over one's own reasoning.
